one_line_idea: Binary masks are a category error for smoke: segmentation error concentrates in a penumbra band that tracks optical thickness, not annotation noise.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Smoke is a volumetric participating medium with no material surface, yet dense-prediction benchmarks represent it with binary masks that assert a crisp spatial extent. [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant error source in smoke segmentation may be representational (forcing a boundary where none exists) rather than perceptual (failing to see the smoke).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel disagreement between any trained model and its ground truth is a monotonic function of local optical transmittance: errors concentrate where transmittance is intermediate, and this dependence persists across architectures because it is a property of the label representation, not the model.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On synthetic smoke renders with known per-pixel transmittance, plotting model-vs-label disagreement against transmittance will show a sharp unimodal peak at intermediate transmittance for every architecture tested; if disagreement is instead flat or architecture-specific, the hypothesis is false.
why_important: If most residual error is representational, the field's effort on bigger backbones for smoke/fire segmentation is misdirected, and the fix is changing the output space (scalar transmittance fields), which is cheap by comparison.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Soft matting for smoke exists, but a systematic architecture-independent attribution of error to the binary representation itself, using physically known transmittance as the controlled variable, may not have been done.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render a small synthetic smoke dataset with ground-truth density (any volumetric renderer), threshold density at a fixed level to create binary labels, train two or three standard segmentation models, and regress per-pixel error against known transmittance.
main_risk: Synthetic smoke may not transfer: the error-vs-transmittance relationship could be an artifact of the renderer rather than a property of real smoke imagery.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Smoke segmentation is treated as a standard hard segmentation task where better features and more data will close the gap to crisp-object performance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotator thresholds may be consistent enough that the binary representation is effectively well-defined, making the penumbra error a small, bounded term rather than the dominant one.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take any pretrained smoke or general segmentation model, run it on a handful of synthetic renders with known transmittance, and check within a day whether the error histogram concentrates at intermediate transmittance.

one_line_idea: Smoke annotators implicitly choose a personal opacity threshold, so inter-annotator disagreement is predictable from local contrast alone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Different annotators draw different smoke boundaries. [HYPOTHESIS] This disagreement may not be random noise but the deterministic consequence of each annotator applying a different internal opacity threshold to the same underlying percept.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Inter-annotator variance at a pixel is a monotone function of how slowly opacity changes across that pixel (the local opacity gradient); annotators agree where opacity changes fast and diverge where it changes slowly, with individual annotators being self-consistent in their threshold across images.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] In a multi-annotator smoke labeling study, a single per-annotator threshold parameter fit on a subset of images will predict that annotator's boundaries on held-out images better than a per-image noise model; failure of the one-parameter model to transfer falsifies the hypothesis.
why_important: If disagreement is a one-parameter threshold family, then multi-rater smoke labels can be losslessly compressed to (soft map, threshold set), and training targets can be constructed that are annotator-invariant.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Annotator modeling exists in medical imaging, but a threshold-family generative model of annotator behavior specifically for participating media, with cross-image self-consistency tests, may be unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Commission or reuse multi-annotator labels on a small smoke image set, fit per-annotator threshold models against an estimated soft opacity map, and test threshold stability across images versus a permutation baseline.
main_risk: Estimating the latent soft opacity map from real images without ground truth may be circular, since the map itself comes from a model or from annotator aggregation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Annotator disagreement on amorphous classes is treated as label noise to be averaged away by majority voting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may use shape completion and semantic reasoning (this is a plume, so it extends here) rather than pointwise opacity thresholds, which would break the one-parameter model.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Have three people label ten smoke images at two sittings; check whether each person's boundary sits at a consistent level set of a soft smoke map estimated by any off-the-shelf matting model.

one_line_idea: Boundary-aware losses presuppose that boundaries exist; on amorphous classes they may actively harm learning.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Boundary-weighted and boundary-refinement losses are widely used in segmentation to sharpen edges. [HYPOTHESIS] For classes without physical boundaries (smoke, flame fringes, infiltrative lesion margins), these losses may force the model to invent arbitrary crisp contours, hurting both accuracy and calibration.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There is a dissociation: adding boundary-weighted loss terms improves segmentation of crisp-boundary classes while degrading soft-boundary classes in the same dataset and training run, because the loss injects a false prior about label geometry.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] In a controlled ablation on a mixed dataset containing both crisp and amorphous classes, the sign of the boundary-loss effect will differ by class type; if the effect has the same sign for both, the hypothesis is false.
why_important: Boundary losses are near-default components; identifying a class-conditional harm would change standard practice for every hard domain in this territory and suggest class-adaptive loss weighting.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Boundary losses are usually evaluated on aggregate metrics; a per-class-type dissociation analysis framed as testing the boundary-existence assumption may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched models with and without a boundary-weighted term on one dataset containing both object classes and smoke or lesion classes; compare per-class soft-boundary-region error and calibration.
main_risk: The effect size may be small relative to run-to-run variance, requiring several seeds to resolve.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Sharper boundaries are always better; boundary losses are considered a safe, broadly beneficial addition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Even amorphous classes are evaluated against crisp annotations, so a loss that mimics the annotator's arbitrary crispness may still improve benchmark scores despite being epistemically wrong.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one model twice (with and without boundary loss) on a small smoke-plus-objects subset for a few epochs and compare error restricted to a dilated band around soft boundaries.

one_line_idea: The extent of a fire region in an image is partly a camera property: predictions may track exposure settings more than physical fire size.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Flame appearance in an image depends strongly on exposure time, gain, gamma, and sensor saturation, because flames are light emitters spanning a huge dynamic range. [HYPOTHESIS] Fire segmentation labels and model outputs may therefore encode camera parameters rather than physical combustion extent.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a fixed physical fire, the segmented area produced by trained models varies systematically and substantially with exposure bracketing, and this variation exceeds the variation across genuinely different fires of similar size, making single-image fire extent an ill-posed target.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On exposure-bracketed captures (or HDR renders re-exposed synthetically) of identical scenes, predicted fire area will be a monotone function of exposure with large relative amplitude; if predicted area is stable across brackets, the hypothesis is false.
why_important: Downstream users (fire monitoring, spread estimation) consume predicted extent as physical measurement; if it is exposure-dominated, deployed systems are reporting camera settings, which is a safety-relevant failure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Robustness studies usually perturb weather or style; treating the camera response function as the primary confounder of fire extent, with bracketed-capture methodology, may be unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or render exposure-bracketed sequences of controlled flames, run several pretrained fire segmentation models, and quantify predicted-area sensitivity to exposure versus sensitivity to actual flame size manipulations.
main_risk: Controlled bracketed fire footage may be hard to obtain safely; synthetic re-exposure may not perfectly emulate sensor saturation behavior.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Fire is considered one of the easier amorphous targets because of its distinctive color and brightness, and extent estimates are assumed roughly physical.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Saturated flame cores may dominate masks and be exposure-stable over the realistic bracket range, leaving only a thin exposure-sensitive fringe of little practical consequence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply synthetic exposure and gamma transforms to existing fire images and measure predicted-area drift of an off-the-shelf model within hours.

one_line_idea: Supervising with soft alpha mattes instead of binary masks changes what the encoder learns, not just what the head outputs.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] The choice between binary and soft supervision for smoke is usually framed as an output-format choice; it may actually determine whether the backbone learns a physically meaningful density-like representation at all.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A backbone trained with soft alpha supervision develops internal features from which smoke optical density is linearly decodable, while a binary-supervised twin of identical architecture and data does not, demonstrating that supervision format shapes representation depth, not just the decision layer.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Linear probes for continuous density on frozen features will show a large accuracy gap between soft-supervised and binary-supervised twins; if probes perform equally, supervision format only affects the head and the hypothesis is false.
why_important: It answers whether the field can retrofit soft outputs onto binary-trained foundations, or whether hard-domain-capable models must be soft-supervised from the start, which changes data collection priorities.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Probing studies compare pretraining objectives; comparing label quantization levels as the manipulated variable for representation formation in dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train twin models on identical synthetic smoke renders, one on binarized labels and one on continuous alpha; freeze both; fit linear probes to predict held-out true density; compare probe error.
main_risk: Probe results on synthetic data may not indicate what happens at foundation-model scale with heterogeneous supervision.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Output representation is a head-level detail; the backbone learns general features regardless of label format.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Binary labels at scale, with boundary pixels acting as implicit soft targets under augmentation jitter, may already force density-sensitive features into the backbone.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe an existing binary-trained smoke model for density decoding on synthetic renders; if density is already linearly decodable, the strong version of the hypothesis dies immediately.

one_line_idea: Models inherit a blob prior from annotators and systematically erase the fractal, multi-connected fine structure of real smoke.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Turbulent smoke exhibits fine filamentary, approximately self-similar structure across scales. [HYPOTHESIS] Human annotators produce simplified, mostly simply-connected blobs, and models trained on them may reproduce the blob statistics rather than the physical geometry.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The boundary complexity (for example, estimated fractal dimension or perimeter-to-area scaling) of predicted smoke masks matches the annotation distribution and is significantly lower than that of physically accurate mattes of the same scenes, and this gap persists even when models have sufficient resolution to represent the fine structure.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On scenes where high-fidelity ground truth is obtainable (synthetic renders or chroma-keyed smoke), predicted masks will show boundary-complexity statistics matching human annotations, not physics; equality with physics falsifies the hypothesis.
why_important: Applications that need fine structure (dispersion modeling, source localization from wisp geometry) cannot use models that structurally smooth it away; it also identifies annotation style as a hard ceiling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Using boundary-geometry statistics as a lens for annotation-bias inheritance in amorphous segmentation may be unexplored; most bias studies focus on semantic or demographic bias.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compose real chroma-keyed smoke plumes over backgrounds to get exact alpha mattes, have annotators label the composites, train on annotations, and compare boundary-complexity distributions among physics, annotations, and predictions.
main_risk: Boundary complexity estimators are resolution-sensitive; conclusions could be confounded by mask resolution rather than learned priors.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Prediction smoothness is attributed to architectural limits (downsampling, CRF-like smoothing), not to inherited annotation style.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Architectural smoothing may indeed dominate: a model trained on physically exact mattes might produce equally blobby output, implicating capacity rather than labels.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare perimeter-to-area scaling of an existing benchmark's annotations against a small set of chroma-keyed smoke mattes to first establish that the annotation-physics gap even exists.

one_line_idea: Smoke and fire leaderboard rankings may be artifacts of the binary-mask representation: rankings could invert under transmittance-aware evaluation.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] If binary masks are a lossy projection of a soft physical quantity, then benchmark rankings computed on binary IoU may not be stable properties of the models but artifacts of the projection.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-scoring existing model families on the same test scenes with a soft, transmittance-aware metric (computed against synthetic or matting-derived soft ground truth) will produce a ranking with low rank correlation to the binary-IoU ranking, indicating that current leaderboards measure threshold placement rather than perception quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Rank correlation between binary-IoU ranking and soft-metric ranking across at least eight models will be low or even negative; a high rank correlation falsifies the claim that the representation drives the ranking.
why_important: Benchmarks steer years of method development; if the ranking is representation-fragile in hard domains, the community may have been selecting for the wrong properties.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Metric-sensitivity analyses exist for crisp segmentation; a representation-change stress test specifically for participating-media benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a test set with soft ground truth (synthetic renders plus chroma-keyed composites), evaluate a diverse zoo of pretrained smoke segmentation models under both binary IoU and a soft error metric, and compute rank correlation.
main_risk: Public pretrained smoke models may be too few or too similar to give a meaningful ranking comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] IoU rankings are treated as robust indicators of relative model quality within a task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model quality differences may be so large that they dominate any representational effect, keeping rankings stable under metric change.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate three or four available models under binary and soft metrics on a small synthetic set; if the ordering is already unstable at this scale, escalate to a full study.

one_line_idea: Fixing an operational opacity threshold may collapse expert disagreement about smoke extent, showing the ambiguity is definitional, not perceptual.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] It is unknown whether disagreement about smoke extent among humans reflects perceptual limits (people cannot see where smoke ends) or definitional vagueness (people disagree about what counts as smoke being present).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When annotators are given an operationalized task definition (mark the region where an object behind the smoke would be attenuated by at least a stated visible amount, with visual anchors), inter-annotator disagreement drops by a large factor relative to free-form instructions, demonstrating the ambiguity is mostly definitional and therefore removable by protocol.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] A within-subjects annotation study comparing free-form versus operationalized instructions will show a large reduction in disagreement area under the operationalized protocol; no reduction falsifies the definitional account.
why_important: If ambiguity is definitional, the field can standardize an operational definition and recover crisp evaluation; if perceptual, soft representations are unavoidable. The experiment decides which research program is correct.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Instruction-manipulation experiments are common in psychophysics but appear rare as a tool for diagnosing segmentation benchmark ambiguity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a two-condition annotation study on the same smoke images with counterbalanced order, measure per-pixel disagreement under each instruction condition, and compare.
main_risk: Operationalized instructions may be too hard to follow without reference tools, adding a new source of noise that masks the effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Smoke boundary ambiguity is treated as inherent to the stimulus and not addressable by annotation protocol design.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Perceptual estimation of attenuation may itself be highly variable across people, so even a precise definition would not reduce disagreement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pilot with three annotators and ten images under both instruction styles; a day of labeling suffices to see whether disagreement shrinks materially.

one_line_idea: Inside a transparent object, foundation-model features may encode the background seen through it better than the object itself.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pixels on a transparent object are photometric mixtures dominated by transmitted background light. [HYPOTHESIS] Vision foundation models may therefore represent glass regions as their background content, making transparent objects representationally invisible rather than merely hard to segment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A linear probe on frozen foundation-model features restricted to pixels inside transparent objects decodes the background category with high accuracy but decodes glass-versus-not-glass poorly, and this asymmetry is far weaker for opaque objects, establishing background dominance in the representation.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Probe accuracy for background identity inside glass regions will substantially exceed probe accuracy for the transparency attribute itself; if transparency is decoded as well as background, the invisibility account is false.
why_important: It distinguishes an information-extraction failure (fixable with better heads or fine-tuning) from a representational absence (requiring different pretraining signals), which determines where effort should go for all transparent-object tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Probing studies of foundation features focus on semantics, depth, or geometry; probing for the transparency attribute versus transmitted content as competing hypotheses may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a probe dataset from transparent-object images with masks, extract frozen features from two or three foundation backbones, train linear probes for (a) glass presence and (b) background class within glass regions, and compare.
main_risk: Probe conclusions depend on layer choice and pooling; a careless probing setup could mistake decodability differences for representational absence.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Foundation features are assumed to be general-purpose enough that transparent objects are hard mainly at the decoding or data level.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transparency might be encoded in subtle non-linear feature combinations that linear probes miss, in which case the deficit is probe-side, not model-side.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run the two probes on one backbone and a few hundred images; the asymmetry, if real, should be visible within a day of compute.

one_line_idea: Transparent-object segmentation may run almost entirely on contour and context, collapsing disproportionately when the silhouette is occluded.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Models appear to segment glass by finding its outline and contextual placement (a cup on a table) rather than surface evidence, but the degree of reliance is unquantified and its failure signature under occlusion is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Occluding a fixed fraction of an object's silhouette degrades transparent-object segmentation much more than opaque-object segmentation matched for size and class frequency, because interior surface evidence exists for opaque objects but is near-absent for glass.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The occlusion-performance curve for transparent objects will fall significantly more steeply than the matched opaque curve; parallel curves falsify the contour-dependence claim.
why_important: Robotic manipulation and household perception involve heavy occlusion; if glass perception is silhouette-only, cluttered-scene failure is structural and predictable, and sensor or temporal remedies become necessary rather than optional.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Occlusion robustness is studied for recognition; a controlled occlusion dose-response comparison isolating the transparency attribute in dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired evaluation sets by compositing calibrated occluders over matched transparent and opaque instances, sweep occlusion fraction, and compare degradation slopes across several models.
main_risk: Matching opaque and transparent instances for all nuisance factors (size, texture, scene) is difficult; poor matching would confound the slopes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Transparent objects are hard uniformly; occlusion is assumed to hurt all categories roughly equally.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models may exploit subtle interior cues (refraction distortions, specular streaks) more than assumed, flattening the transparent-occlusion curve.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Composite synthetic occluder bars over a small transparent-object test set at three occlusion levels and measure one pretrained model's degradation slope in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Do segmentation models use refraction at all? Rendered index-of-refraction ablations can measure it directly.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Refraction is the physically defining optical signature of transparent solids, producing systematic background distortion. [HYPOTHESIS] Current models may be entirely blind to this cue, relying instead on highlights and contours, but no direct measurement of refraction reliance exists to my knowledge (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model performance on rendered transparent objects is statistically indistinguishable between physically correct refraction and a counterfactual render with the index of refraction set to one (no distortion, other cues preserved), demonstrating zero use of the defining physical cue.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The performance delta between refraction-on and refraction-off matched renders will be near zero for standard models; a significant delta falsifies the blindness claim and instead quantifies refraction reliance.
why_important: If models ignore refraction, there is a concrete, physically grounded information source left on the table, motivating pretraining or augmentation that makes refraction discriminative rather than yet another architecture iteration.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cue-ablation via physically based rendering is used for shading and shadow studies; an index-of-refraction ablation targeting segmentation seems unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render paired scenes (identical geometry, lighting, materials except index of refraction), evaluate several pretrained models on both, and test the paired performance difference.
main_risk: Removing refraction also subtly changes highlights and caustics unless carefully controlled, contaminating the ablation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] It is loosely assumed that networks pick up whatever cues are useful, including distortion patterns, given enough data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Refraction may be a genuinely weak cue at typical image resolutions against unstructured backgrounds, so blindness to it would be information-theoretically rational rather than a model failure.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Render a dozen paired scenes in an open-source renderer and compare one model's masks across the pair the same day.

one_line_idea: Specular highlights may be the load-bearing shortcut for glass detection; cross-polarized imagery could collapse current models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Specular highlights on glass are strong, sparse photometric events, and they can be physically removed with cross-polarization. [HYPOTHESIS] Trained models may depend on highlights far more than on any other transparency cue, making them brittle to lighting geometries and polarizing filters that suppress highlights.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Suppressing specular highlights (via cross-polarized capture or highlight-removal rendering) causes a catastrophic, disproportionate drop in transparent-object segmentation while leaving opaque-object segmentation nearly intact, identifying highlights as the dominant learned cue.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The highlight-suppressed performance drop for glass will exceed the drop for matched opaque objects by a large factor; comparable drops falsify highlight dominance.
why_important: Highlight geometry is a property of the light rig, not the object; deployment environments (diffuse lighting, polarizing windshields) routinely suppress highlights, so this brittleness would predict real-world failures invisible on benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Highlight reliance is discussed qualitatively; a controlled polarization-based cue-removal study for dense transparent-object prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture a small paired dataset with parallel and cross polarization of scenes containing glass and matched opaque objects; evaluate pretrained models on both conditions.
main_risk: Cross-polarization changes global contrast slightly, requiring careful normalization to isolate the highlight factor.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Glass segmentation models are assumed to integrate multiple cues, with no single point of failure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Contour and context cues may carry enough signal that highlight removal is survivable, especially for large objects.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use software highlight suppression on existing glass benchmark images and check one model's degradation within hours, before investing in polarized capture.

one_line_idea: A pixel on glass belongs to two surfaces at once; single-label segmentation is structurally wrong, and part of measured error is this representational deficit.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Through a transparent surface, a camera ray intersects at least two scene surfaces (the glass and the background), yet standard semantic segmentation assigns exactly one label per pixel. [HYPOTHESIS] A quantifiable fraction of measured error on transparent classes is not misperception but the impossibility of encoding two truths in one label.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] When the output space is expanded to two depth-ordered labels per pixel (front layer, rear layer), a fixed backbone recovers a large portion of what single-label evaluation scored as error, isolating the representational component of transparent-object failure.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The same features decoded into a two-layer output will resolve a substantial share of single-label errors on glass regions; if two-layer decoding yields no reduction, the representational-deficit account is false.
why_important: It partitions the error budget between perception and representation for an entire object class, telling the field whether to fix models or fix the task definition.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Layered scene representations exist in matting and de-occlusion literatures, but using them as an error-accounting instrument for transparent-class benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate or synthesize a modest set with front and rear labels through glass, train two heads on one frozen backbone (single-label and two-layer), and compare error attributable to glass regions under each output space.
main_risk: Two-layer annotation is expensive and itself ambiguous for complex stacks of transparency (glass behind glass).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Errors on glass pixels are read as the model failing to see glass, not as the label space failing to admit the correct answer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmarks may already resolve the conflict consistently by convention (always label the glass), making single-label ground truth self-consistent enough that little error is representational.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually inspect a sample of glass-region errors from any pretrained model and categorize how many are plausible rear-layer answers; a high fraction justifies the full study.

one_line_idea: Depth foundation models place glass at the background depth; segmentation models sharing those backbones may inherit the glass-invisible prior.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Monocular depth estimators commonly see through glass, reporting the rear surface. [HYPOTHESIS] Since dense-prediction systems increasingly share pretrained backbones with depth-supervised objectives, a see-through prior may propagate from depth training into segmentation behavior in a measurable, causal way.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The per-image degree to which a shared backbone's depth head sees through a given glass instance predicts the segmentation head's failure on that same instance, across instances and scenes, indicating a common upstream representation choice rather than independent errors.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Instance-level correlation between depth see-through magnitude and segmentation miss rate will be strong and positive on shared-backbone systems and much weaker across systems with unrelated backbones; absence of the correlation falsifies inheritance.
why_important: If failure is inherited through pretraining objectives, curing it requires intervening on pretraining signals, and depth-based pretraining choices for embodied stacks would need rethinking for households full of glass.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cross-task failure correlation as evidence of prior inheritance between depth and segmentation heads appears unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take a multi-task or shared-backbone model with depth and segmentation heads, compute per-glass-instance depth see-through scores and segmentation errors, and test correlation against a mixed-backbone control.
main_risk: Correlation could be driven by shared image-level difficulty (thin, clean glass is hard for everything), requiring careful difficulty controls.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Task heads are assumed to fail independently; depth quirks are treated as depth problems.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Segmentation fine-tuning may fully overwrite the glass-related geometry of the representation, breaking any inherited coupling.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one shared-backbone model and thirty glass instances, scatter-plot depth see-through against segmentation IoU per instance; visible structure justifies the controlled study.

one_line_idea: Glass and smoke fail differently: geometric boundaries with weak photometrics jitter, photometric gradients without geometry smear; a two-axis failure taxonomy is testable.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Hard domains are lumped together as low-contrast, but glass has physically sharp boundaries with weak image evidence while smoke has no boundary at all; whether these produce statistically distinct failure signatures is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Prediction error decomposes differently by domain: transparent objects show high boundary-localization variance with low extent bias (jitter), while smoke shows low localization variance with high extent bias (systematic shrinkage or growth), and this signature separates the two domains under a blind statistical test.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] A classifier given only error-decomposition statistics (bias and variance of boundary displacement) will distinguish glass errors from smoke errors well above chance; failure to separate falsifies the taxonomy.
why_important: A validated failure taxonomy lets remedies be assigned by failure type rather than by domain, potentially unifying method development across medical, smoke, and transparency subfields.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Boundary-error decomposition into bias and variance components as a domain-diagnostic signature seems undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute signed boundary-displacement distributions for several models on glass and smoke test sets, extract bias and variance summaries per instance, and test separability with a simple classifier and permutation control.
main_risk: Boundary displacement is ill-defined exactly where ground truth is soft, so the smoke-side measurement needs a defensible operationalization.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Hard domains fail because of low contrast, a single shared cause with a single family of fixes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both domains may show mixtures of jitter and shrinkage dominated by per-dataset annotation habits, swamping any physical signature.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Plot signed boundary-displacement histograms for one model on one glass and one smoke dataset; visually distinct shapes justify formal testing.

one_line_idea: Static single-image transparent-object segmentation may sit near an information-theoretic ceiling that humans also cannot beat without motion.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] It is unresolved how much of the model-human gap on transparent objects reflects model deficiency versus an intrinsic information limit of static images, since humans normally exploit motion parallax and active head movement for transparency.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under matched static-image forced-choice conditions (patch-limited context, no motion), human accuracy at detecting glass drops toward current model accuracy, implying much of the reported gap comes from evaluation regimes that implicitly grant humans richer viewing conditions.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] A psychophysics study with context-controlled static presentations will show human-model agreement on which instances are impossible; if humans stay far above models under matched conditions, the ceiling account is false and the deficit is model-side.
why_important: It sets the correct target: if static images are information-starved, the field should move to temporal or polarization sensing rather than chase static benchmarks toward an unreachable ceiling.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Human-model comparisons under carefully matched information conditions exist for recognition, but seemingly not for transparency-specific dense perception.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design a two-alternative forced-choice glass-present task with patch-size-controlled stimuli for humans and models, and compare psychometric curves as context radius grows.
main_risk: Matching information access between humans and models is subtle (foveation, viewing time), and mismatches would bias the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Humans are assumed to be far better at seeing glass in any format, so model headroom on static benchmarks is assumed large.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Humans may exploit high-level scene reasoning that survives static presentation, keeping them well above models even under matched viewing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run an informal pilot with a few subjects on a hundred patch-controlled stimuli against one model in a single afternoon session.

one_line_idea: Training on randomly sampled single raters versus the majority vote may not add noise but shift boundary placement in a consistent direction.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Medical segmentation ground truth is typically a single expert's contour or a merged consensus, while true inter-rater variability is substantial for infiltrative structures. [HYPOTHESIS] The common assumption that single-rater training equals consensus training plus noise may hide a systematic geometric bias.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on per-image randomly sampled raters converge to a boundary that is systematically offset (for example toward higher-contrast image gradients) relative to models trained on consensus labels, because the loss interacts asymmetrically with rater disagreement structure rather than averaging it out.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On any multi-rater dataset, the signed distance between single-rater-trained and consensus-trained model boundaries will show a consistent nonzero mean over structures, not a zero-mean scatter; zero-mean scatter falsifies the systematic-bias claim.
why_important: Nearly all clinical segmentation training data is single-rater; a directional artifact of that choice would propagate a hidden bias into deployed contours used for treatment planning.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Multi-rater learning work targets modeling the distribution; the geometric direction of single-rater-induced bias appears uncharacterized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, train matched models under the two label regimes with multiple seeds, compute signed boundary displacement fields between their predictions, and test the mean against zero.
main_risk: The effect may vary in sign across anatomies, requiring stratified analysis and more data than one dataset provides.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Rater sampling is treated as label noise that large datasets and averaging losses wash out.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Cross-entropy and Dice may genuinely average boundary positions when disagreement is symmetric, leaving no directional trace.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune one model under both regimes on a small multi-rater subset and inspect signed displacement histograms after a day of training.

one_line_idea: The direction of systematic over- or under-segmentation may be set by the loss function, not the data, in a predictable size-dependent way.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Overlap losses like soft Dice are known to behave differently from cross-entropy on small structures. [HYPOTHESIS] What remains unestablished is a quantitative law: that the sign and magnitude of extent bias is a function of loss type and structure size distribution, independent of anatomy and modality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For each common loss (cross-entropy, soft Dice, focal, combinations), there exists a characteristic size-dependent bias curve (predicted-over-true volume ratio versus structure size) that replicates across unrelated datasets, so extent bias is loss-determined and therefore correctable analytically.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Bias curves measured on synthetic phantoms will predict, without refitting, the bias curves measured on real medical datasets for the same losses; failure to transfer falsifies loss-determinism of the bias.
why_important: Volume estimates drive clinical decisions (growth assessment, dose planning); a loss-induced size-dependent bias is a correctable systematic error currently absorbed silently into models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Loss pathology papers exist, but a transferable quantitative bias law validated from phantoms to real data may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic phantoms with controlled size distributions and blur, train under each loss, fit bias curves, then measure whether these curves predict bias on two unrelated real datasets.
main_risk: Real-data bias may be dominated by annotation conventions rather than loss, drowning the loss signature.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Extent bias is treated as a data property or an architecture quirk to be fixed empirically per task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Interactions between loss and class imbalance handling (sampling, weighting) may make the bias non-transferable across pipelines.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train small models under two losses on one synthetic phantom family and check within a day whether size-dependent bias curves differ in the predicted directions.

one_line_idea: Model uncertainty maps may fail to correlate with where human experts actually disagree, because they measure the wrong kind of doubt.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Uncertainty estimation methods output per-pixel doubt, and papers often imply these maps indicate clinical ambiguity; whether they actually align with the spatial structure of inter-rater disagreement is an open empirical question with a directly available test.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The spatial correlation between standard uncertainty maps (softmax entropy, ensemble variance, dropout variance) and true inter-rater variance maps is weak, because model uncertainty tracks feature-space unfamiliarity and decision-margin geometry, while rater disagreement tracks anatomical ambiguity, and these are different fields.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Across structures in a multi-rater dataset, rank correlation between model uncertainty and rater variance at matched pixels will be low; consistently high correlation falsifies the misalignment claim.
why_important: Clinical review triage and quality control increasingly rely on uncertainty maps as ambiguity proxies; if they are misaligned with expert disagreement, that reliance is unsafe.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Individual comparisons exist in scattered forms; a systematic multi-method, multi-structure alignment audit framed as testing what uncertainty measures may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, compute pixelwise rater variance, extract uncertainty maps from several methods on the same images, and quantify spatial alignment with correlation and overlap-of-top-decile analyses.
main_risk: Rater variance estimated from few raters is itself noisy, attenuating measurable correlations and risking a false negative.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Model uncertainty is assumed to be a usable stand-in for ambiguity, especially aleatoric decompositions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In well-calibrated models trained on multi-rater targets, uncertainty may in fact align well; the misalignment may be specific to single-rater training.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one model and one multi-rater structure, overlay top-decile uncertainty pixels on top-decile disagreement pixels and compute overlap in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Predicting rater-percentile contours (p10, p50, p90) as explicit nested targets, and testing when nesting is even valid.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Infiltrative lesion margins elicit graded expert opinion rather than a single contour. [HYPOTHESIS] Representing ambiguity as quantile contours presumes rater contours are approximately nested (ordered by a single conservativeness axis); the validity of that presumption is untested and determines whether quantile masks are a coherent target.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Rater contour families are approximately nested for boundary-graded ambiguity (margins) but violently non-nested for topological ambiguity (include or exclude a satellite lesion), so quantile-mask methods are valid on a measurable subset of cases identifiable in advance.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] A nestedness index computed over rater sets will be bimodal across cases, separating margin-type from topology-type ambiguity; a unimodal distribution falsifies the two-regime account.
why_important: It gives the field a validity criterion for an increasingly popular ambiguity representation, preventing quantile methods from being applied where they are mathematically incoherent.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Probabilistic segmentation methods produce diverse samples, but a formal empirical test of rater-set nestedness as a representational validity condition appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a nestedness index (fraction of rater-pair inclusion violations), compute it across all structures in one or more multi-rater datasets, and cluster cases by index against ambiguity-type labels assigned by a radiologist.
main_risk: Nestedness may depend on rater count; with few raters the index has high variance.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Ambiguity is implicitly treated as one-dimensional conservativeness, which is exactly what quantile masks encode.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Almost all real disagreement might turn out to be margin-type, making the validity concern practically moot.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute inclusion-violation rates over rater pairs for a handful of structures from any multi-rater dataset in a few hours of scripting.

one_line_idea: Models may learn institution-specific contouring conventions so strongly that the annotating institution is decodable from predicted masks alone.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Contouring conventions (how far to extend margins, whether to include edema) differ across institutions and protocols. [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on multi-site data may encode these conventions as if they were anatomy, creating a style shortcut that inflates in-distribution scores and corrupts cross-site transfer.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A classifier can predict the training-label institution from the geometry of predicted masks alone (no image input) at well above chance, demonstrating that convention style, not just anatomy, is baked into predictions.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask-only institution classification accuracy will be far above chance for models trained on site-heterogeneous labels; chance-level accuracy falsifies the style-encoding claim.
why_important: If predictions carry annotation style, cross-site performance drops are partly label-side artifacts, and harmonizing conventions could recover performance without any modeling work, reshaping how federated medical datasets are built.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Site effects on images (scanner signatures) are studied; site effects flowing through label conventions into prediction geometry seem largely unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train segmentation models on data from multiple sites, generate masks on a common held-out image pool, and train a mask-geometry classifier for source-site prediction with permutation controls.
main_risk: Image-side site signatures could leak into masks through anatomy differences in patient populations, confounding the style attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Cross-site degradation is attributed almost entirely to image distribution shift (scanners, protocols), not label conventions.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Convention differences may be too subtle relative to anatomical variation for a mask-only classifier to detect.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Using any two-site multi-rater or multi-cohort dataset, train a quick mask-geometry classifier on ground-truth contours themselves; if even ground-truth style is not separable, the model-level claim is unlikely.

one_line_idea: Ambiguous pixels and difficult pixels are different populations, possibly anti-correlated, and current methods conflate them.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] A pixel can be ambiguous (experts disagree) or difficult (experts agree but models fail); the two are conceptually distinct, yet uncertainty research and hard-example mining treat a single hardness axis. Whether the two populations overlap, and how much, is measurable and unknown to me (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Ambiguity (rater variance) and difficulty (model error at rater-consensus pixels) occupy substantially different image regions, with modest or even negative spatial correlation, implying that methods optimizing hard pixels are spending capacity on irreducible ambiguity while missing tractable difficulty.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Joint maps on multi-rater data will show the top-decile ambiguity set and top-decile difficulty set overlapping far less than chance-matched expectation; strong overlap falsifies the two-population claim.
why_important: Loss weighting, curriculum, and active learning all allocate resources by a single hardness score; splitting the axis could redirect that allocation toward pixels where improvement is actually possible.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] The aleatoric-epistemic distinction exists in theory, but a direct empirical cartography of ambiguity-versus-difficulty using rater consensus as the anchor appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a multi-rater dataset, compute per-pixel rater variance and per-pixel model error restricted to consensus pixels, then measure overlap and correlation between the two top-decile sets across images and models.
main_risk: Model error and rater variance are both concentrated near boundaries, which could produce spurious overlap unless boundary distance is controlled.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Hard pixels are hard for everyone; a single difficulty ranking underlies sample weighting practice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In heavily ambiguous anatomy the two sets may genuinely coincide because ambiguity causes label noise which causes model error at the same locations.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Produce the two decile maps for a handful of images from one multi-rater dataset and one pretrained model in a day.

one_line_idea: Lesion-level detection ranking versus voxel-overlap ranking: the field may be selecting architectures that reliably miss small lesions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Voxel-overlap metrics like Dice weight structures by volume, so small lesions contribute almost nothing to aggregate scores. [HYPOTHESIS] Years of architecture selection by overlap metrics may have produced a lineage of models optimized to sacrifice small-lesion detection, a clinically inverted priority.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-ranking a broad set of published-style architectures by lesion-level detection F-score produces a materially different ordering than Dice ranking on the same data, and the divergence grows as lesion size shrinks, indicating that benchmark-driven selection has been optimizing against clinical priorities on small findings.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Rank correlation between Dice-based and lesion-detection-based orderings across many models will be low on small-lesion-rich data; high correlation falsifies the metric-divergence claim.
why_important: Missing small lesions (early metastases, microbleeds) is among the most consequential clinical errors; if metric choice has been steering the field away from them, that is a correctable systemic failure.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Metric critiques exist; a longitudinal model-zoo re-ranking framed as measuring the selection pressure exerted by metrics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a diverse zoo of segmentation models on a lesion-rich dataset under both metrics, stratify by lesion size, and quantify ranking divergence.
main_risk: Public model zoos may share training pipelines, limiting the diversity needed to observe divergent rankings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Dice improvements are assumed to translate monotonically into clinical utility.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern pipelines often add lesion-wise losses and evaluation already; the divergence may have been quietly fixed in current practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take three existing models with public weights for one lesion task and compare their orderings under the two metrics in a day.

one_line_idea: Boundary voxels are physical mixtures (partial volume): regressing mixture fractions may beat classification and match physics on phantoms.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Finite scanner resolution means boundary voxels contain a mixture of tissues (partial volume effect), so a hard class label at the boundary is physically wrong. [HYPOTHESIS] Treating boundary voxels as mixture-fraction regression targets aligns the label space with image formation and may remove a systematic boundary-placement bias.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On phantoms with known sub-voxel geometry, classification-trained models place boundaries with a systematic offset determined by the point-spread function, while mixture-fraction regression recovers the true interface with near-zero bias, and the correction transfers to real scans as improved volume accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Phantom experiments will show a nonzero, PSF-dependent boundary bias for classification that vanishes under fraction regression; equal bias under both falsifies the label-space account.
why_important: Sub-voxel bias compounds into clinically meaningful volume errors for small structures; a physics-aligned label space would fix it at the formulation level rather than by post-hoc calibration.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Partial volume is heavily studied in reconstruction and tissue quantification, but as an explanation and fix for deep segmentation boundary bias it may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate scans of digital phantoms with known interfaces and PSF, train classification and fraction-regression twins, and measure signed boundary error and volume bias for both.
main_risk: Real annotations do not provide fraction targets, so the real-data validation must rely on volume consistency arguments rather than direct supervision.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Partial volume is treated as an image artifact to be robust against, not as evidence that the segmentation label space is misspecified.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may already learn a soft internal representation that compensates for PSF, leaving little bias for the new label space to remove.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Measure whether an existing model's boundary placement on synthetic blurred phantoms shifts predictably as the blur kernel widens; the presence of PSF-dependent bias is the gating observation.

one_line_idea: Promptable segmentation foundation models may exhibit a measurable snapping field: masks jump to the nearest high-contrast contour regardless of prompt intent on amorphous targets.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Promptable segmentation foundation models (SAM-style) were trained predominantly on discrete objects with visible contours. [HYPOTHESIS] On amorphous targets (smoke, ground-glass opacities), their mask decoders may implement a systematic attraction toward nearby photometric contours, describable as a vector field over prompt positions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For a fixed image, the mapping from click-prompt position to output mask is piecewise constant with basins bounded by photometric contours, and on amorphous regions the basins collapse onto surrounding crisp structures, so the model is structurally incapable of returning the diffuse region regardless of prompt placement.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense prompt-sweep maps on smoke scenes will show output masks dominated by nearby crisp objects for a majority of in-smoke click positions; if in-smoke clicks mostly return smoke-like masks, the snapping account is false.
why_important: Promptable models are becoming annotation and clinical tooling infrastructure; a structural inability to select amorphous regions means those tools silently cannot label exactly the classes this territory cares about.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Prompt-sensitivity studies exist, but a systematic geometric characterization of prompt-to-mask basins as a diagnostic instrument for the object-centric prior may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid-sweep click prompts over images containing smoke and crisp objects, cluster the returned masks, and map basin geometry against photometric contour maps for one or more promptable models.
main_risk: Multi-mask output modes and prompt ensembling may blur the basin structure, requiring careful control of decoding settings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Prompting failures on diffuse targets are seen as fixable with better prompt engineering or a few fine-tuning examples.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Larger prompt sets (boxes, multiple positive clicks) may already be able to select diffuse regions reliably, making the single-click pathology practically irrelevant.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run a coarse prompt sweep on five smoke images with one public promptable model and visually inspect basin maps within hours.

one_line_idea: Prompt-output variance as a free ambiguity detector: the spread of masks under prompt jitter may track true target ambiguity.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Foundation models expose a new observable that classical segmenters lack: the distribution of outputs across prompts. Whether this distribution carries calibrated information about target ambiguity (rater disagreement, soft extent) is unknown and directly testable.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of masks produced under small prompt perturbations correlates strongly with independent ambiguity measures (multi-rater variance in medical images, opacity gradation in smoke), making promptable models zero-shot ambiguity meters even where their point predictions are poor.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Across structures with known rater variance, prompt-jitter mask variance will rank-correlate substantially with rater variance; near-zero correlation falsifies the ambiguity-meter claim.
why_important: Ambiguity estimation currently requires multi-rater data or bespoke probabilistic models; a zero-shot proxy from existing foundation models would make ambiguity auditing cheap across all hard domains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Prompt sensitivity is usually reported as a robustness defect; reinterpreting and validating it as an ambiguity signal may be a new framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For structures in a multi-rater medical dataset, sample prompts within each structure, compute mask variance across prompts, and correlate with rater variance across the same structures.
main_risk: Prompt variance may mostly reflect the snapping pathology (idea B-025), which is model idiosyncrasy, not target ambiguity; the two must be disentangled.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Prompt sensitivity is noise to be engineered away, not signal to be measured.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ambiguity as experts experience it may be driven by knowledge (pathology semantics) invisible to a promptable vision model, decoupling the two variances.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute prompt-jitter variance for twenty structures with known rater disagreement and scatter-plot the two quantities in a day.

one_line_idea: A gradient snapping coefficient: quantifying how strongly mask decoders relocate semantic boundaries onto photometric gradients.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] In infiltrative disease, the clinically correct boundary often lies where the image shows no gradient, and the strongest gradient lies elsewhere. Models may systematically relocate boundaries onto gradients, but the field lacks a standardized measurement of this tendency.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Each model family has a stable, measurable gradient snapping coefficient (mean displacement of predicted boundary toward the nearest strong image gradient, normalized by gradient distance), which is larger for foundation models pretrained on natural images than for models trained from scratch on medical data, and which predicts infiltrative-margin error better than overall Dice does.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Snapping coefficients estimated on controlled stimuli will transfer to predict per-case infiltrative-margin errors on real data; if the coefficient is unstable across stimuli or fails to predict real errors, the construct is falsified.
why_important: A standardized snapping metric would let practitioners audit any model for gradient bias before clinical use, and would quantify a suspected cost of natural-image pretraining in medical dense prediction.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Edge bias is discussed anecdotally; a portable, validated coefficient with cross-dataset predictive power appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct stimuli where annotation boundary and photometric gradient are controllably separated (synthetic lesions with displaced texture edges), measure boundary displacement for several models, and validate the coefficient against real infiltrative-case errors.
main_risk: Separating annotation boundary from gradient in real training data is impossible retrospectively, so the construct rests on synthetic-to-real transfer.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Boundary placement quality is captured adequately by boundary metrics; no distinct snapping construct is needed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Snapping may be context-dependent (varying with texture, scale, class) rather than a stable per-model scalar, undermining the coefficient framing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Generate a dozen displaced-edge synthetic cases and measure whether two models show consistent, distinct displacement patterns within a day.

one_line_idea: Foundation-model failure on hard domains may be predictable from the mismatch between target scale statistics and pretraining object-scale priors.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Web-image pretraining exposes models to a particular distribution of object scales and aspect statistics; medical structures, smoke plumes, and glass panes occupy very different regions of that distribution, and the failure rate may be a smooth function of the mismatch.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Zero-shot and lightly fine-tuned foundation-model performance on a target class is predictable from a scale-prior mismatch score (divergence between the class's scale-context statistics and the pretraining distribution), across medical, smoke, and transparency domains, better than domain identity predicts it.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Regressing per-class performance against mismatch scores across many classes will explain a large share of variance and beat a domain-label-only baseline; failure to beat domain labels falsifies scale-mismatch as the operative factor.
why_important: A predictive mismatch score would tell practitioners in advance which clinical or industrial targets foundation models will fail on, and quantify what pretraining data reweighting must fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Transferability estimation exists for classification; a scale-prior account with cross-domain predictive validation for dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate scale-context statistics for a few dozen target classes across the three domains, evaluate one or two foundation models per class, and fit the mismatch regression with cross-validation.
main_risk: The pretraining distribution of public foundation models is only partially known, forcing the mismatch score to rely on proxies.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Foundation-model transfer failure is attributed to appearance shift (modality, texture) rather than to scale-statistics mismatch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance shift and scale mismatch are correlated in practice, and appearance may dominate once properly measured.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For ten classes with obviously different scale profiles, check whether zero-shot performance ordering matches the mismatch ordering in a two-day probe.

one_line_idea: Scaling pretraining data may asymptote for transparency and smoke because the missing ingredient is label ontology, not pixels.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] The scaling paradigm assumes more data monotonically improves all downstream tasks. For classes whose correct description requires concepts absent from the pretraining label space (per-pixel multi-layer opacity), scale may buy little, but no scaling curve stratified by this property exists to my knowledge (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across checkpoints of increasing pretraining scale, performance on opaque-object segmentation grows steadily while performance on transparency and participating-media segmentation plateaus early, because the pretraining objective never demands the multi-layer photometric decomposition those classes require; the gap is ontological, not statistical.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale-versus-performance curves stratified by class type will show diverging slopes, with hard-domain curves flattening while matched-difficulty opaque curves keep rising; parallel curves falsify the ontological-gap account.
why_important: It determines whether the hard domains in this territory will be solved for free by scaling or require deliberately different supervision, which is a strategic question for the whole field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Scaling studies report aggregate transfer; stratifying scaling curves by a representational-requirement taxonomy may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Use publicly released checkpoint series of one model family at multiple pretraining scales, evaluate frozen-feature probes on matched opaque and hard-domain segmentation tasks, and compare slope trajectories.
main_risk: Public checkpoint series confound scale with recipe changes; clean scale isolation may require training small model series from scratch.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Remaining hard-domain gaps are expected to close with the next generation of larger models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Emergent capabilities could appear at scales beyond the tested range, making an observed plateau a local artifact.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe two checkpoints (small and large) of one family on one opaque and one transparency task; a visibly differential improvement pattern justifies the full curve.

one_line_idea: Text-prompted segmentation may ground count nouns better than mass nouns, disadvantaging smoke, fluid, and tissue categories linguistically.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Natural language distinguishes count nouns (a cup) from mass nouns (smoke, water, tissue), and vision-language training pairs images mostly with object-centric captions. [HYPOTHESIS] Language-grounded dense predictors may inherit a count-noun advantage that penalizes exactly the amorphous categories of this territory, independent of visual difficulty.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Controlling for visual difficulty, open-vocabulary segmentation accuracy is systematically lower for mass-noun categories than count-noun categories, and the gap shrinks when mass nouns are rephrased as pseudo-count expressions (a cloud of smoke, a pool of water), demonstrating a linguistic rather than visual origin.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The rephrasing manipulation will recover a significant fraction of the mass-noun gap; no recovery under rephrasing falsifies the linguistic-origin claim.
why_important: If part of the hard-domain gap is linguistic interface artifact, prompt-side fixes are nearly free, and vision-language pretraining corpora could be rebalanced for mass-noun grounding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Linguistic typology as a causal variable in dense prediction performance appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble category pairs matched for visual segmentation difficulty (measured by supervised-model performance) differing in noun type, evaluate open-vocabulary models under original and rephrased prompts, and test the interaction.
main_risk: Matching visual difficulty across noun types is hard; residual visual confounds could masquerade as linguistic effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Open-vocabulary failures on stuff classes are attributed to visual amorphousness, with the language side assumed neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Caption corpora may contain plenty of mass-noun supervision (scene descriptions), so the grounding gap may not exist.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one open-vocabulary segmenter on a handful of mass-noun categories with original versus pseudo-count prompts and compare masks the same day.

one_line_idea: A linear-separability audit of frozen foundation features across hard domains: is the deficit in the features or in the decoders?
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Hard-domain failures are usually reported at the system level, leaving unknown whether frozen foundation features already fail to separate smoke, glass, and lesion pixels from confusers, or whether separable features are being wasted by decoders trained with misspecified objectives.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Linear separability of hard-domain pixels in frozen feature space is substantially lower than for matched-frequency opaque classes, and crucially, the separability gap accounts for most of the end-to-end performance gap, locating the failure in representation rather than decoding.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Across several backbones, per-class linear-probe accuracy will predict per-class end-to-end fine-tuned accuracy with high fidelity for hard domains; if fine-tuned accuracy greatly exceeds what probes predict, the deficit is decoder-side and the representational account is false.
why_important: It is the triage question for the whole territory: whether to invest in new pretraining signals (features are the bottleneck) or in output-space and loss redesign (decoding is the bottleneck).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Probing is standard for semantics; using probe-versus-finetune gap decomposition as a bottleneck-location instrument across these specific hard domains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a fixed set of hard and control classes, measure frozen linear-probe accuracy and full fine-tune accuracy per class per backbone, and analyze how much of the hard-domain gap the probe gap explains.
main_risk: Linear probes underestimate nonlinear decodability, potentially misattributing decoder-recoverable structure to representational absence.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Foundation features are assumed near-universal; hard-domain work concentrates on decoders, prompts, and fine-tuning recipes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Small nonlinear heads might recover almost everything linear probes miss, collapsing the claimed representational gap.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run linear and small-MLP probes for three hard classes and three control classes on one backbone in a day; a large probe-type discrepancy immediately reshapes the interpretation.

one_line_idea: Under ambiguity, foundation segmenters may output confident all-or-nothing masks with a detectable bimodal signature instead of graded responses.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] When the target is ambiguous (faint smoke, subtle ground-glass opacity), a well-behaved estimator should produce graded output; foundation segmenters may instead bifurcate between confident empty and confident full masks depending on imperceptible input changes, a behavioral signature of ambiguity mishandling that has not been characterized (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Across an ambiguity-graded stimulus continuum, foundation-model mask areas follow a bimodal distribution with a sharp transition zone, while both human responses and properly calibrated probabilistic models transition smoothly, and the transition point is unstable across seeds and augmentations.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Measuring predicted-area distributions along controlled fade-in continua (smoke opacity ramps, lesion contrast ramps) will show bimodality indices far exceeding those of human observers on the same continua; smooth unimodal transitions falsify the claim.
why_important: All-or-nothing behavior under ambiguity is the worst failure mode for safety applications (fire detection, screening), because it defeats downstream thresholding and risk stratification entirely.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Psychometric-function-style characterization of dense predictors along ambiguity continua appears rare; the bimodality signature as a model-audit statistic may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct opacity and contrast ramp stimuli by compositing, sweep them through several models, record predicted-area trajectories, and compare bimodality statistics against human psychometric data on the same stimuli.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts along the ramp could themselves cause the discontinuities, requiring photometrically careful stimulus construction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Softmax outputs are assumed to degrade gracefully as evidence weakens.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some architectures may genuinely produce graded masks along such continua, making the pathology model-specific rather than a foundation-model property.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Build one ten-step opacity ramp and run two models across it, plotting mask area per step, within a single day.

one_line_idea: IoU on soft-boundary targets mostly measures whether the model guessed the annotator's threshold, not whether it perceived the medium.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Two models with identical estimates of a soft quantity but different binarization behavior can receive very different IoU scores against thresholded annotations; the size of this thresholding term in real benchmark scores is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For amorphous-class benchmarks, a large fraction of between-model IoU differences is eliminated when each model is evaluated at its per-image oracle threshold, demonstrating that the leaderboard signal is dominated by threshold agreement rather than perceptual quality.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Oracle-threshold evaluation will compress between-model IoU spreads on smoke and lesion benchmarks by a large factor while leaving crisp-class spreads nearly unchanged; equal compression across class types falsifies the claim.
why_important: If leaderboards on hard domains are threshold lotteries, method development is being steered by noise, and a decoupled evaluation (soft estimate quality plus thresholding policy) would redirect the field.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Oracle-threshold analyses exist in detection calibration contexts; applying threshold-decoupled evaluation as a benchmark-forensics tool for amorphous segmentation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-evaluate a set of pretrained models on one amorphous and one crisp benchmark under fixed-threshold and per-image oracle-threshold protocols, comparing spread compression.
main_risk: Oracle thresholds overfit per image; conclusions need a held-out threshold-selection variant to be persuasive.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] IoU differences on any benchmark are read as perception-quality differences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may differ genuinely in soft-estimate quality and the threshold term may turn out to be small once measured.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For three models on one smoke dataset, compare fixed versus oracle-threshold IoU spreads in an afternoon of evaluation scripting.

one_line_idea: Boundary-quality metrics on fractal boundaries may rank mask-smoothing hyperparameters, not models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Boundary metrics (boundary F-measure style) compare boundary bands at a chosen tolerance. [HYPOTHESIS] When the true boundary is fractal-like (smoke wisps, infiltrative margins), these metrics may become dominated by the interaction between tolerance radius and mask smoothness, so that post-hoc smoothing changes scores more than model substitution does.
