core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On amorphous-class benchmarks, applying simple morphological smoothing sweeps to a fixed model's masks moves its boundary-metric score across a range wider than the score differences among competing published-style models, proving the metric primarily measures smoothing policy in this regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The smoothing-induced score range for one model will exceed the between-model range on amorphous classes but not on crisp classes; failure of this ordering falsifies the pathology claim.
why_important: Boundary metrics are the standard rebuttal to IoU criticisms; showing they collapse on exactly the classes where boundaries are contested removes the field's fallback metric and forces new evaluation design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Sensitivity of boundary metrics to tolerance is known folklore; a quantified smoothing-versus-model-substitution comparison on amorphous classes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several models on amorphous and crisp benchmarks, sweep morphological smoothing per model, and compare within-model score ranges to between-model ranges under a boundary metric.
main_risk: Choice of smoothing family could be accused of cherry-picking; multiple smoothing operators are needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Boundary metrics are treated as the more trustworthy complement to region metrics precisely on boundary-critical classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At sensible fixed tolerances the metric may remain model-discriminative, with smoothing effects staying second-order.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Take one model on one smoke dataset, sweep three smoothing levels, and check score movement against two other models' scores in hours.

one_line_idea: Metric forensics: the training loss may leave identifiable morphological fingerprints in predicted masks.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] If losses induce characteristic output morphologies (blob bias, hole suppression, boundary sharpening), then masks carry information about their training objective; establishing this would both prove that losses distort morphology and enable auditing of black-box segmentation services.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A classifier trained on mask morphology statistics alone (no images) can identify which of several standard losses produced the masks, at high accuracy, across architectures and datasets, demonstrating that objective choice systematically shapes output geometry independent of data.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-architecture, cross-dataset loss identification from masks will remain far above chance; chance-level generalization falsifies the fingerprint claim.
why_important: It converts a vague worry (losses bias shapes) into a measurable, transferable signature, informs loss selection for morphology-sensitive clinical tasks, and enables black-box audits of deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Model-attribution forensics exists for generative images; loss-attribution forensics for segmentation masks appears novel.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a grid of models (several losses by several architectures by two datasets), extract morphology features from predictions on a common pool, and evaluate leave-one-architecture-out loss classification.
main_risk: Fingerprints may be dataset-specific, vanishing under cross-dataset transfer and reducing the result to an unsurprising in-domain effect.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Losses affect scores, but final mask geometry is assumed to be dominated by data and architecture.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern combined losses may homogenize morphology, leaving fingerprints too weak for reliable attribution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train two small models differing only in loss on one dataset and test same-day whether a simple classifier separates their output masks.

one_line_idea: Mean scores hide bimodal competence: on hard domains, models may either nail or completely miss cases, making the mean a fiction.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Aggregate metrics presume per-case performance is unimodal around the mean. On hard domains, anecdotal experience suggests all-or-nothing behavior, but the distributional shape of per-case scores has not been systematically compared across easy and hard domains (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-case score distributions on transparency, smoke, and small-lesion tasks are strongly bimodal (a success mode and a total-failure mode), while matched easy-domain distributions are unimodal, implying that reporting means on hard domains misrepresents model behavior and hides the failure mode that matters.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Bimodality statistics of per-case scores will separate hard from easy domains across many models; unimodal hard-domain distributions falsify the claim.
why_important: Bimodal competence changes everything downstream: deployment risk is about the failure-mode probability, not the mean; and method comparison should compare failure-mode rates, which mean-based leaderboards cannot see.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Per-case variance is occasionally reported; a cross-domain study of score distribution shape as a diagnostic of failure structure may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect per-case scores for many models across hard and easy benchmarks, fit mixture models to each distribution, and compare bimodality across domain types.
main_risk: Score bounded-ness (IoU in unit interval) distorts distribution shape; analysis needs care to avoid artifacts of the bounded support.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A higher mean score is read as uniformly better behavior across cases.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Bimodality might reflect dataset composition (two latent difficulty groups) rather than model failure structure, requiring difficulty-conditioned analysis.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Histogram per-case IoU for one model on one transparency dataset and one ordinary dataset in an hour and inspect modality.

one_line_idea: Test downstream utility directly: matting-style perceptual error may predict task usefulness of smoke masks better than IoU does.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Segmentation metrics are proxies for downstream utility, but for participating media the proxy validity is untested: a mask can have good IoU yet destroy the downstream estimate (fire spread direction, visibility assessment) and vice versa.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In a simulated downstream pipeline (for example, estimating plume growth rate or visibility maps from masks), soft matting-style error measures of the mask predict downstream estimate error substantially better than binary IoU does, establishing that the field's default metric is a poor utility proxy exactly where the domain is hard.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Across many mask-quality perturbations, correlation between downstream error and matting error will substantially exceed correlation with IoU; comparable correlations falsify the proxy-invalidity claim.
why_important: Metric validity is upstream of everything: if IoU is a weak utility proxy for this territory, benchmark-driven progress is partially illusory and utility-anchored evaluation should replace it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Downstream-utility validation of segmentation metrics exists in some medical planning studies; doing it for participating-media applications may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define one or two concrete downstream computations over smoke masks, generate mask variants spanning quality dimensions (extent bias, boundary softness, topology errors), and correlate each candidate metric with downstream error.
main_risk: Conclusions are conditional on the chosen downstream tasks; critics can dispute their representativeness.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Higher IoU is assumed to imply higher usefulness for whatever comes next.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For extent-driven downstream tasks, IoU may be a perfectly adequate proxy, confining the critique to boundary-sensitive applications.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Simulate one downstream computation with synthetically perturbed masks and rank correlations among three metrics in a day.

one_line_idea: Statistical power audit: hard-domain subsets of benchmarks may be too small for most published ranking differences to be meaningful.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Hard cases (small lesions, faint smoke, clean glass) are minorities within datasets, so metric differences on them rest on few samples. [HYPOTHESIS] The effective sample size on hard subsets may be so low that many between-method differences celebrated in the literature are statistically indistinguishable, but no systematic power audit of this territory exists to my knowledge (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Bootstrap and permutation analysis of standard benchmarks will show that on hard-domain subsets, the minimal detectable effect at conventional confidence exceeds the typical between-method difference, meaning the benchmarks cannot support the conclusions drawn from them at current test-set sizes.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Confidence intervals on hard-subset metric differences between adjacent leaderboard entries will overlap heavily for most pairs; tight non-overlapping intervals falsify the underpowering claim.
why_important: It quantifies how much of perceived progress on exactly the hard cases is statistical noise, and prescribes concrete test-set sizes for future benchmarks in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Power analyses exist for classification benchmarks; a hard-subset-focused power audit for dense prediction in these domains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For two or three public benchmarks, define hard subsets by objective criteria, bootstrap metric differences between multiple model pairs, and report minimal detectable effects versus observed effects.
main_risk: Defining hard subsets post hoc invites selection critique; criteria must be pre-registered and objective.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A benchmark improvement of the usual magnitude is treated as real without uncertainty quantification.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Per-pixel correlations within cases complicate the effective sample size question in both directions; careful hierarchical bootstrapping might reveal adequate power after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Bootstrap the hard-subset score difference between two public models on one benchmark in a day and inspect interval overlap.

one_line_idea: On some hard benchmarks, models may already disagree with the ground truth less than single human annotators do, making further leaderboard gains noise-fitting.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Every benchmark has an annotation-quality ceiling: once model-GT disagreement falls below rater-rater disagreement, the metric stops measuring perception. Which hard-domain benchmarks have crossed this ceiling is unknown and decisive for interpreting current results (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On mature hard-domain benchmarks, top models' disagreement with consensus is already at or below the disagreement of individual expert annotators with that same consensus, implying the remaining leaderboard spread reflects fitting annotation idiosyncrasy rather than perception gains.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Collecting a multi-rater subset for a benchmark and comparing model-consensus versus rater-consensus disagreement will show the crossover for at least some benchmarks; if models remain far above single-rater disagreement everywhere, the ceiling concern is currently moot.
why_important: Identifies which benchmarks are exhausted instruments, redirects effort toward new evaluation targets, and prevents publication incentives from rewarding annotation-noise overfitting in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Ceiling analyses exist for classification datasets; systematic ceiling measurement for hard-domain dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Commission independent re-annotation of a modest benchmark subset by several qualified raters, compute rater-consensus and model-consensus disagreement distributions, and locate each benchmark relative to its ceiling.
main_risk: Qualified re-annotation (especially medical) is expensive and rater recruitment may bottleneck the study.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Benchmark headroom is assumed real: better scores mean better models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hard-domain benchmarks may have much more headroom than intuition suggests, with models still far below single-rater consistency.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate thirty cases of one smoke benchmark with three raters and place two public models relative to the rater spread within a week.

one_line_idea: Fixed-threshold evaluation penalizes calibrated soft predictions: models honest about ambiguity may score worse than overconfident ones.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Standard evaluation binarizes predictions at a fixed threshold before scoring. A model producing faithful graded output on ambiguous regions may be scored below a model that outputs confident wrong crispness, creating an anti-calibration selection pressure whose magnitude is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] There exist realistic prediction pairs (one calibrated-soft, one overconfident-crisp, equal underlying information) where standard pipelines systematically score the overconfident model higher on hard domains, and this ordering reverses under proper-scoring-rule evaluation, proving benchmarks select against honesty about ambiguity.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Constructed and naturally occurring model pairs will show the ranking inversion between thresholded-IoU and proper-score evaluation on ambiguous regions; absence of inversions falsifies the anti-calibration pressure claim.
why_important: If benchmarks punish calibrated ambiguity reporting, the field is training away the very property that safety-critical deployments in this territory need most.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Proper scoring rules are standard in probabilistic forecasting; a demonstration that segmentation benchmark protocol actively selects against calibration on ambiguous classes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take soft outputs from probabilistic and deterministic models on ambiguous benchmarks, evaluate under thresholded-IoU and proper scores restricted to ambiguity bands, and count ranking inversions.
main_risk: Defining ambiguity bands without multi-rater data requires proxies that critics may dispute.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Thresholding before scoring is considered a neutral formality of evaluation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In practice overconfident and calibrated models may differ in underlying quality too, making clean inversions rare outside constructed examples.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Construct the synthetic prediction pair on real images and demonstrate or fail to demonstrate the scoring inversion in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Smoke segmenters may be global haze-statistics detectors: histogram manipulations could flip predictions with local structure fixed.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Smoke changes global image statistics (contrast reduction, color cast) in ways cheaply detectable without localizing anything; models may have learned these global shortcuts, meaning their masks are driven by scene-level statistics rather than pixel-level evidence.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Manipulating global color and contrast statistics toward or away from smoke-typical values, while keeping local structure fixed, will move predicted smoke masks substantially (appearing in smoke-free regions or vanishing from smoky ones), demonstrating global-statistic reliance incompatible with genuine dense perception.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Histogram-matched counterfactual images will change predicted smoke area by a large factor despite unchanged local content; invariance under the manipulation falsifies the shortcut claim.
why_important: Global shortcuts predict exactly the deployment failures that matter (fog false alarms, backlit scenes), and quantify how much of benchmark performance is scene classification masquerading as segmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Shortcut studies target classification; global-versus-local cue decomposition for dense smoke prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build counterfactual pairs by histogram matching smoke-free images to smoke statistics and vice versa, run several models, and quantify mask changes attributable to the global manipulation.
main_risk: Histogram manipulation is not perfectly local-structure-preserving; edge cases need photometric care.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Dense predictors are assumed to rely on local evidence at each pixel by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Receptive fields do include global context legitimately; some global sensitivity is proper Bayesian context use, so the experiment must distinguish reasonable context weighting from outright shortcut dominance.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Histogram-match ten clear images toward smoke statistics and check one model's false smoke area the same day.

one_line_idea: Fire segmentation may depend on sensor saturation: HDR imagery without clipped pixels could break current models.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Flames commonly saturate consumer sensors, producing clipped white-yellow regions. [HYPOTHESIS] Models may have learned saturation artifacts (clipping plateaus, blooming) as the primary fire cue, which would fail on HDR or properly exposed professional footage precisely in high-stakes monitoring deployments.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Fire segmentation performance drops disproportionately on unclipped renditions of the same scenes (HDR tone mappings preserving flame texture), and the learned models' most salient features localize on clipping boundaries rather than combustion structure, establishing saturation as a load-bearing shortcut.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Paired clipped versus unclipped renditions will show a large performance asymmetry and attribution maps concentrated on clipping artifacts; parity across renditions falsifies the saturation-shortcut claim.
why_important: Professional fire-monitoring cameras increasingly avoid clipping; a saturation dependence would mean models validated on consumer footage silently fail on the better sensors used in deployment.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Exposure robustness is studied broadly; identifying sensor clipping as the specific learned cue for fire may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture or synthesize HDR fire scenes, produce clipped and unclipped low-dynamic-range renditions, evaluate models on both, and run attribution analysis on the difference.
main_risk: Tone-mapping choices introduce their own distribution shift, which must be controlled with non-fire scenes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Fire is assumed easy because of distinctive color; sensor pipeline effects are ignored in the fire-segmentation literature I am aware of (unverified).
why_it_might_be_wrong: Flame color and flicker texture may carry enough signal that models survive unclipped renditions with modest degradation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Apply inverse-clipping simulation (compressing highlights) to existing fire images and measure one model's degradation within hours.

one_line_idea: When intensity and shape cues conflict in medical images, models may follow intensity even where shape says otherwise; the conflict point is measurable.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Lesion segmentation can rely on intensity contrast or on shape context; these usually agree in training data, hiding which cue models actually use. Constructed cue-conflict stimuli can reveal the hierarchy, which matters because pathology often presents with atypical intensity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On cue-conflict phantoms (lesion-shaped regions with inverted or nulled contrast, and lesion-intensity regions with implausible shapes), models overwhelmingly follow intensity, and the intensity dominance measured on phantoms predicts real-world failure on atypical-presentation cases such as isointense lesions.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The phantom-measured intensity-dominance index will correlate across models with error on curated atypical-intensity clinical cases; no correlation falsifies the diagnostic value of the conflict test.
why_important: Isointense and atypically presenting lesions are precisely the ones humans also miss; knowing that models are pure intensity followers would quantify a shared blind spot and motivate shape-pathway supervision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cue-conflict methodology is established in texture-shape classification work; a medical dense-prediction version with clinical validation linkage may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate cue-conflict stimuli by editing real scans (contrast manipulation within anatomically plausible masks), measure per-model cue-following rates, and correlate with performance on a held-out atypical-presentation case set.
main_risk: Edited scans risk leaving editing artifacts that models detect, contaminating the conflict measurement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Deep segmenters are assumed to integrate shape and context significantly, exceeding classic intensity thresholding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern models with large receptive fields may genuinely use shape context, showing mixed cue-following that defeats the simple dominance narrative.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Create ten contrast-nulled lesion phantoms and check whether two models still find the lesions in a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke may be predicted wherever fire context appears: pasting fire-adjacent context into clean scenes could conjure phantom smoke masks.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Training scenes for smoke overwhelmingly contain co-occurring context (flames, forests, chimneys, emergency lighting); models may segment smoke partly from this context rather than from smoke evidence, producing hallucinated masks in smoke-free but fire-adjacent scenes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Compositing fire-context elements into verified smoke-free scenes induces smoke predictions in regions with no smoke-like appearance, with the induced area growing with context strength, demonstrating a quantifiable context-hallucination pathway distinct from appearance confusion.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Context-injection composites will produce significant phantom smoke area across models, spatially disconnected from injected elements; near-zero phantom area falsifies the context-hallucination claim.
why_important: False alarms in fire monitoring have real costs (suppression dispatch, alarm fatigue); a context pathway would explain false alarms that appearance-based analysis cannot, and would indict co-occurrence statistics in training data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Context reliance is studied for object recognition; measuring context-induced dense hallucination for safety classes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a composite test set injecting graded fire context into smoke-free scenes, run several smoke segmenters, and measure phantom mask area versus context dose with compositing-artifact controls.
main_risk: Compositing artifacts may themselves trigger predictions; artifact-only control composites are essential.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] False positives are attributed to smoke-like appearance (fog, steam), not to semantic context priming.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense predictors may be more locally grounded than feared, with context influencing confidence but not creating masks from nothing.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Paste flame crops into ten clean landscape images and check two models for phantom smoke in an afternoon.

one_line_idea: Video-compression artifacts may be a learned smoke cue: recompression could move masks more than scene changes do.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Much smoke and fire footage originates from surveillance systems and online video with strong lossy compression, and codecs treat diffuse moving textures distinctively. [HYPOTHESIS] Models may have learned codec signatures (blocking, mosquito noise around soft gradients) as smoke evidence, which would make predictions bitrate-dependent in deployment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Predicted smoke masks change substantially under recompression sweeps (varying codec and bitrate on identical content), with the direction of change consistent with codec-artifact reliance, and models trained on high-compression sources show the largest sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Mask instability across recompression will exceed a tight threshold and correlate with training-source compression statistics; bitrate-invariant masks falsify the codec-cue claim.
why_important: Deployment cameras differ wildly in encoding; codec-dependent perception would produce unexplained site-to-site performance swings and is invisible to standard benchmark practice, which fixes the encoding.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Compression robustness is studied generically; identifying codec artifacts as a positive learned cue for a specific safety class may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Recompress a fixed evaluation set across codecs and bitrates, measure per-model mask drift, and compare drift against content-change baselines.
main_risk: Bitrate changes also remove genuine fine smoke texture; disentangling artifact-cue loss from evidence loss needs synthetic smoke with known ground truth.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Compression is treated as benign nuisance noise handled by augmentation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Standard augmentation pipelines may already include compression, having inoculated models against codec dependence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Recompress ten test videos at three bitrates and measure one model's mask drift the same day.

one_line_idea: Texture-shape bias may be amplified at segmentation boundaries: per-pixel stylization tests could show boundary decisions are texture-driven where shape should rule.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Texture bias in classification networks is established. [HYPOTHESIS] For dense prediction, the interesting question is spatial: whether texture reliance intensifies near boundaries, exactly where hard domains (infiltrative margins, wispy smoke) offer no reliable texture, which would explain concentrated boundary failure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Stylization interventions (texture replacement with shape preserved) perturb predictions disproportionately within a narrow band around boundaries relative to interiors, and this boundary texture-dependence is largest in the hard domains of this territory, revealing a spatially structured shortcut invisible to image-level bias measures.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Prediction-change maps under stylization will concentrate in boundary bands with an interior-to-boundary ratio far below one; spatially uniform perturbation sensitivity falsifies the boundary-amplification claim.
why_important: It localizes the texture-bias problem to where hard domains actually fail, and implies boundary-specific remedies (shape-biased boundary decoding) rather than global stylization augmentation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Texture-bias literature reports image-level effects; a per-pixel spatial decomposition of cue reliance in dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply structure-preserving stylization to evaluation images, compute per-pixel prediction change, stratify by distance to ground-truth boundary, and compare across domains and models.
main_risk: Stylization inevitably alters some shape-adjacent cues (local contrast), requiring multiple stylization operators to triangulate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Texture bias is an image-level property, treated with global augmentation; spatial structure of the bias is not part of the discussion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary regions might show high sensitivity to any perturbation simply because decisions there sit near the margin, requiring margin-controlled analysis to avoid triviality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Stylize five images, plot the prediction-change-versus-boundary-distance curve for one model in a day.

one_line_idea: Single-frame smoke benchmarks may leak motion information through blur signatures, inflating reported single-image capability.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Frames extracted from video retain motion blur, and moving smoke produces characteristic directional blur patterns. [HYPOTHESIS] Purportedly single-image smoke segmentation may exploit these temporal residues, overstating what is achievable from genuinely static observation and misleading sensor-design conclusions.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models evaluated on deblurred or fast-shutter versions of benchmark frames lose a substantial share of their smoke segmentation performance, revealing that part of the claimed single-frame capability is hidden temporal information rather than static appearance understanding.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Performance on blur-removed frames will drop significantly more for smoke than for static-object classes in the same frames; equal drops falsify the motion-leakage claim.
why_important: System designers choose between single-frame and temporal architectures based on benchmark evidence; leakage-corrupted evidence leads to under-provisioned temporal modeling in deployed safety systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Benchmark leakage studies focus on duplicates and label leakage; motion-blur as an information side channel in single-frame evaluation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct paired evaluations with original frames and deblurred counterparts (algorithmic deblurring validated on static content), compare smoke-class degradation against static-class degradation across models.
main_risk: Deblurring introduces its own artifacts; a static-class control and multiple deblurring methods are needed to attribute the drop correctly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Single-frame evaluation is assumed to measure static-appearance understanding by construction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: At typical surveillance shutter speeds smoke motion blur may be negligible, making the side channel empty.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one model on ten original versus deblurred frames and check the smoke-specific drop within a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke versus steam versus fog: current models may be undifferentiated haze detectors, and a confusability audit would expose the semantic emptiness.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Steam, fog, dust, and smoke are optically similar participating media with different safety semantics. [HYPOTHESIS] Models labeled as smoke detectors may be detecting generic haze, with class identity supplied by dataset context rather than perception, which would make their semantic label scientifically and practically misleading.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On a balanced cross-media test set, smoke segmenters will fire near-equally on steam, fog, and dust once scene context is neutralized, and their discrimination ability will collapse toward chance under context randomization, showing the smoke label reflects dataset co-occurrence, not media identification.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Context-neutralized discrimination between smoke and other media will be near chance for current models; strong above-chance discrimination falsifies the haze-detector claim.
why_important: The smoke-versus-steam distinction is the difference between an alarm and a false alarm in industrial settings; knowing whether the distinction is perceptual or contextual determines what data must be collected next.

one_line_idea: Pixelwise calibration can be perfect while extent estimates are wildly miscalibrated, because dense errors are spatially correlated; extent-level calibration is the missing target.

[HYPOTHESIS] This mismatch may allow models to pass pixel-level calibration audits while producing region-area estimates whose confidence intervals are meaningless, which is what downstream users actually consume.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models with near-perfect pixelwise expected calibration exhibit severe miscalibration of derived quantities (total area, structure count, extent percentile), with realized coverage of area confidence intervals far below nominal, because correlated errors violate the independence implicitly assumed when aggregating pixel probabilities.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On any hard-domain dataset, area confidence intervals derived from pixelwise-calibrated probabilities will show realized coverage dramatically below nominal; near-nominal coverage falsifies the correlated-error account.
why_important: Clinical volume estimates and fire-extent reports rely on aggregated dense outputs; a systematic gap between pixel and aggregate calibration is a silent safety defect that current audit practice cannot detect.

fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute realized area-interval coverage for one temperature-scaled model on one dataset in a few hours.

one_line_idea: On hard domains, feature-space distance to training data may predict errors better than the model's own confidence does.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Softmax confidence is the default error predictor, but on transparency and participating media the inputs are systematically unlike training data in ways confidence may not register; whether representation-space novelty is a better error predictor specifically in these domains is untested (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-pixel and per-region error on hard domains is predicted more accurately by feature-space distance to the training distribution than by predictive entropy or max-probability, and the advantage of the distance signal grows with domain hardness, reversing the usual ranking observed on easy in-distribution data.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Error-prediction AUROC comparisons across easy and hard test strata will show a crossover favoring feature distance on hard strata; uniform superiority of confidence falsifies the crossover claim.
why_important: Selective prediction and human-in-the-loop triage in medical and safety applications need reliable error flags precisely on hard inputs; knowing which signal to trust where is directly actionable.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Model confidence, possibly recalibrated, is treated as the best available self-assessment everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fine-tuned models may internalize hard-domain statistics well enough that confidence remains the better signal even there.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute both predictors for one model on one hard dataset and compare AUROC in a day.

one_line_idea: Do learned aleatoric uncertainty terms actually match observer disagreement? Multi-rater data offers a direct validity test that may fail.
problem: [VERIFIED PRIOR WORK - general] Heteroscedastic loss formulations produce per-pixel aleatoric uncertainty estimates, widely interpreted as capturing irreducible data ambiguity. [HYPOTHESIS] Whether these learned terms quantitatively match the actual observer-disagreement distribution at each pixel has a direct test on multi-rater data, and the match may be poor because the training signal conflates ambiguity with model misfit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Learned aleatoric maps correlate only weakly with true rater-variance maps, and the learned term absorbs epistemic error wherever the model underfits, so the aleatoric label on these outputs is quantitatively unjustified in hard domains.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Pixel-matched comparisons on multi-rater data will show low correlation and systematic inflation of learned aleatoric values in regions of model misfit; strong correlation with rater variance falsifies the conflation claim.
why_important: The aleatoric-epistemic decomposition guides data-collection versus model-improvement decisions; if the decomposition is invalid where it matters most, those decisions are being made on fiction.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] The decomposition is theoretically debated; a direct empirical validity audit against observer distributions in medical dense prediction may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train heteroscedastic models on multi-rater data using single sampled raters, compare learned aleatoric maps to held-out rater variance, and manipulate model capacity to test whether the aleatoric term shrinks as fit improves (it should not, if truly aleatoric).
main_risk: Rater variance from few raters is a noisy target, biasing correlations downward and risking unfair falsification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Learned aleatoric uncertainty is treated as measuring data ambiguity by definition of the loss.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With sufficient capacity and data, the decomposition may become empirically clean, confining the critique to underfit regimes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: The capacity-manipulation check alone (does the aleatoric map change when only model size changes) is runnable in two days and is decisive for the conflation claim.

one_line_idea: Deep ensembles may agree on the same wrong crisp boundary instead of spanning plausible contours, underestimating ambiguity in a systematic direction.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Ensemble spread is the standard epistemic uncertainty proxy, presumed to bracket plausible answers. For structured ambiguity (where truth is a distribution over contours), independently trained members may collapse onto the same attractor (the annotation convention or the strongest gradient), making spread a biased, not just noisy, ambiguity estimator.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On multi-rater structures, ensemble member disagreement is significantly smaller than rater disagreement, and member boundaries cluster tightly around a single mode even when raters are multimodal, demonstrating that ensemble spread systematically underestimates structured ambiguity rather than estimating it noisily.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Spread-versus-rater-disagreement comparisons will show ensembles capturing only a small fraction of rater variance with unimodal member distributions on multimodal cases; ensembles matching rater spread falsify the collapse claim.
why_important: If ensembles cannot represent contour multimodality, the field's default uncertainty tool is structurally blind to the main ambiguity type in this territory, and mask-distribution models become necessary rather than optional.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Ensemble diversity is studied for classification; a geometric comparison of ensemble contour distributions against rater contour distributions may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a deep ensemble on single-rater-sampled labels from a multi-rater dataset, compare member-contour distributions to rater-contour distributions per structure, including modality analysis.
main_risk: Ensemble diversity depends heavily on training stochasticity choices; conclusions need multiple diversity-induction settings.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Ensemble variance is treated as a faithful, if conservative, ambiguity estimate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: With aggressive diversity induction (data resampling, augmentation variation), ensembles may span rater-like distributions after all.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train a small five-member ensemble on one structure type and overlay member contours against rater contours for twenty cases within two days.

one_line_idea: Naive pixelwise conformal prediction for masks may deliver nominal marginal coverage while structure-level coverage is near zero.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Conformal methods give distribution-free marginal coverage guarantees for the score they calibrate. [HYPOTHESIS] Applied pixelwise to dense masks, the guarantee may be satisfied in a way that is useless: per-pixel coverage holds on average while the probability that an entire structure is captured by the prediction set is negligible, a gap practitioners in safety domains are unlikely to appreciate.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pixelwise conformal segmentation on hard domains exhibits the predicted marginal-joint coverage gap at extreme magnitude (nominal per-pixel, near-zero per-structure), and the gap is worst exactly where errors are most correlated (amorphous regions), making structure-level conformal scores a necessary redesign, not a refinement.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Empirical structure-level coverage under pixelwise calibration will be far below nominal on smoke and lesion data; achieving near-nominal structure coverage falsifies the gap-severity claim.
why_important: Conformal wrappers are being marketed as safety layers for medical AI; quantifying how their guarantees can be technically true and practically empty in dense prediction protects against misplaced trust.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] The marginal-joint distinction is mathematically known; measuring its practical magnitude and spatial structure in these hard domains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement pixelwise conformal segmentation on one medical and one smoke dataset, measure per-pixel and per-structure coverage, and map the gap against error-correlation length.
main_risk: Defining structure-level coverage requires choices (full containment versus overlap thresholds) that affect the headline numbers.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A conformal guarantee is treated as delivering the safety semantics users imagine, regardless of the score's granularity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sensible practitioners may already use region-level scores, making the naive pixelwise strawman unrepresentative of practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run pixelwise conformal calibration on one dataset and compute both coverage types in a day.

one_line_idea: Boundary ambiguity wants soft maps; topological ambiguity wants mask sets: a dissociation experiment could establish the representation-ambiguity matching law.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] The field offers two ambiguity representations (per-pixel soft maps and diverse mask samples) without a principled account of when each is adequate; ambiguity type (graded boundary versus discrete structural alternatives) may be the deciding variable, which is testable by dissociation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Downstream decision quality (simulated planning or alarm decisions) shows a double dissociation: soft maps support boundary-graded ambiguity as well as mask sets at lower cost, but fail catastrophically on multimodal structural ambiguity (include or exclude a satellite region), where small diverse mask sets dominate; hence representation should be selected by measured ambiguity modality.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On stratified cases (unimodal versus multimodal rater distributions), the representation-by-ambiguity interaction on downstream utility will be strong and crossed; no interaction falsifies the matching law.
why_important: It would replace ad hoc representation choices with a measurable criterion, unifying probabilistic segmentation work under a decision-theoretic selection rule relevant to every domain in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Both representations exist in prior work; a controlled double-dissociation study tying representation adequacy to ambiguity modality may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate multi-rater cases stratified by rater-distribution modality, feed oracle ambiguity representations of both kinds into fixed downstream decision simulations, and measure utility per stratum.
main_risk: Multimodal-rater cases are rare in available datasets, potentially starving one arm of the dissociation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Richer output representations are assumed generically better, with sampling-based methods treated as the high-end default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Soft maps with post-hoc connected-component reasoning might handle multimodality adequately, erasing the dissociation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Hand-construct a dozen synthetic multimodal and unimodal ambiguity cases and compare oracle representations on one downstream rule in two days.

one_line_idea: Confidence-correctness correlation may invert on transparent objects: models could be most confident exactly where glass fools them.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Selective prediction assumes confidence ranks correctness at least weakly. On transparent objects, the background-dominated appearance may make models confidently perceive the background class, producing not low correlation but inverted correlation between confidence and correctness, which would break abstention frameworks in the worst possible way.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Restricted to transparent-object regions, per-pixel confidence-correctness rank correlation is negative for standard models (higher confidence predicts higher error), because confident background perception is precisely the transparency failure, whereas opaque-region correlations stay positive.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Region-conditional correlation analysis will show sign inversion on glass regions across multiple models; merely weakened positive correlation falsifies the inversion claim.
why_important: Sign inversion is qualitatively worse than miscalibration: abstention mechanisms would systematically keep the wrong pixels; documenting where inversions occur is prerequisite for any safe selective-prediction deployment around glass (robotics, autonomous navigation).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Confidence quality is usually summarized globally; class-conditional sign analysis targeting a physically explainable inversion may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several segmenters on transparent-object benchmarks, compute confidence-correctness correlations within glass regions versus matched opaque regions, and test for sign differences.
main_risk: Ground-truth masks define glass regions, so label errors there directly contaminate the correlation estimate.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Confidence may be miscalibrated but is assumed at least directionally informative everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Models may be visibly uncertain (low confidence) on glass rather than confidently wrong, yielding weak positive correlation and no inversion.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute the two conditional correlations for one model on one glass benchmark in a few hours.

one_line_idea: Calibrating segmentation to asymmetric downstream costs may require spatially varying thresholds that no global calibration can express.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Downstream costs of over- and under-segmentation are asymmetric and spatially heterogeneous (missing tumor margin near a critical organ costs differently than elsewhere). [HYPOTHESIS] Standard practice compresses this into one global threshold; the utility loss from that compression is unquantified and may be large in hard domains where ambiguity is spatially structured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Decision-theoretically optimal segmentation under realistic spatial cost maps requires thresholds varying by location and context, and the utility gap between globally thresholded and spatially cost-calibrated outputs is substantial on ambiguous structures, establishing utility calibration as a distinct problem from probability calibration.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Under simulated but structurally realistic cost maps, spatially varying thresholding of the same probabilistic output will outperform the best global threshold by a large utility margin on hard cases; negligible margins falsify the practical-relevance claim.
why_important: It reframes what calibrated means for deployed dense prediction: probability calibration is insufficient without cost-aware decision layers, a gap directly affecting radiotherapy planning and emergency response mapping.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cost-sensitive learning is classical; quantifying the global-versus-spatial thresholding utility gap for ambiguous dense prediction may be new.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A single operating point per model per task, chosen on validation data, is considered adequate deployment practice.

fastest_falsification_experiment: Simulate one cost map on one dataset with an existing probabilistic model and measure the thresholding utility gap in a day.

one_line_idea: Beer-Lambert attenuation suggests log-transmittance, not alpha, as the natural regression target for smoke; conditioning of the loss landscape may differ measurably.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Light passing through smoke attenuates approximately exponentially with optical depth (Beer-Lambert law), so alpha values compress a huge physical range near saturation. [HYPOTHESIS] Regressing alpha directly may create poorly conditioned gradients in thick-smoke regions, while log-domain targets align the loss geometry with the physical variable, a formulation-level effect testable independent of architecture.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training identical networks to predict log-transmittance instead of alpha yields systematically better recovery of thick-smoke structure and better extrapolation across density regimes on synthetic data with known ground truth, because the target parameterization linearizes the physically multiplicative process.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On renders spanning wide optical-depth ranges, the log-domain twin will dominate in thick-regime error while matching elsewhere; no regime-dependent advantage falsifies the conditioning claim.
why_important: If target parameterization alone shifts hard-regime performance, every participating-media pipeline gains a free improvement, and the result exemplifies aligning label spaces with image formation rather than scaling models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Log-domain processing is standard in physics-based vision; a controlled parameterization study for learned smoke dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render smoke across controlled optical-depth ranges, train twin regressors on alpha versus log-transmittance, and compare regime-stratified errors and cross-regime generalization.
main_risk: Log targets amplify noise in near-transparent regions, potentially trading one regime's accuracy for another's.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Output parameterization is treated as a minor implementation detail relative to architecture and data choices.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may internally learn whatever reparameterization helps, making explicit target transforms redundant at sufficient scale.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train two small twins on one synthetic set and compare thick-regime errors within two days.

one_line_idea: Thin and thick smoke are different physical regimes (single versus multiple scattering); training data may cover one and models may silently fail on the other.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Radiative transfer through participating media transitions from single-scattering-dominated (thin, background visible) to multiple-scattering-dominated (thick, diffusive, self-illuminated) regimes with qualitatively different appearance. [HYPOTHESIS] Datasets and models may be regime-imbalanced in unmeasured ways, and evaluation aggregated across regimes may hide near-total failure in one of them.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model error stratified by physical scattering regime (estimable on synthetic data and approximable on real data via background visibility) shows a sharp regime asymmetry that aggregate metrics conceal, and models trained thin fail thick (and vice versa) far more than smooth interpolation would predict, because the regimes present effectively different visual tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Regime-stratified evaluation will reveal an error ratio between regimes far exceeding what within-regime difficulty variation explains; smooth degradation across the transition falsifies the discrete-regime claim.
why_important: Thick-smoke scenes are the highest-stakes cases (structure fires, pyroCb events); if models are thin-regime specialists, deployed systems fail exactly when needed, and dataset curation needs a physical stratification variable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Radiative-transfer regimes are textbook physics; using them as an evaluation stratification and generalization axis for learned segmentation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render datasets controlled for scattering regime, train per-regime and mixed models, and measure the cross-regime generalization matrix and its asymmetries.
main_risk: Real-image regime estimation is indirect; the real-data arm depends on a visibility-based proxy of contestable accuracy.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Smoke density is treated as a continuous nuisance parameter, with more data assumed to cover the range adequately.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Appearance across the transition may be smooth enough for networks to interpolate, making the regime boundary practically invisible.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one pretrained model on renders from both regimes and inspect the stratified error ratio within days.

one_line_idea: Fire is an emitter, not a reflector: emissive regions violate learned shading priors, and characteristic halo errors around flames may be the fingerprint.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Almost all segmentation training imagery depicts reflective surfaces under external illumination, while flames emit light, illuminating their surroundings and inverting typical shading relationships. [HYPOTHESIS] Models may carry an implicit reflectance assumption whose violation near flames produces structured errors (halos of false positives on illuminated smoke or surfaces, missed flame cores) that are currently unattributed.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Segmentation errors around fires are spatially organized by the flame's illumination field: false positives concentrate on flame-lit surfaces and false negatives inside emission cores, and matched rendered scenes with emissive versus externally lit fire-shaped objects reproduce the error structure, establishing the reflectance prior as the cause.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The emissive-versus-lit rendering contrast will causally reproduce halo error structure across models; identical error patterns for both lighting types falsify the emission-violation account.
why_important: It would explain a family of fire-scene failures mechanistically, guide augmentation with emissive rendering, and generalize to other emitters (welding, headlights, lava) where dense prediction is safety-relevant.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Lighting robustness work exists; isolating emission as a violated prior with rendered causal controls for dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render matched scenes (emissive flame object versus identical shape externally lit), run models, and compare spatial error statistics around the object under both conditions.
main_risk: Renderer realism for flames is limited; sim-to-real transfer of the causal conclusion needs a small real-footage validation arm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Fire-scene errors are attributed to color confusion and dataset scarcity, not to violated illumination priors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Halo errors may be simple appearance confusion (lit smoke looks like flame-colored haze) requiring no prior-violation story.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inspect error maps of one model around twenty real flame images for the predicted halo structure before any rendering investment.

one_line_idea: Polarization may carry the signal RGB lacks for glass and smoke: small polarization probes could beat large RGB foundation models, proving an information gap rather than a model gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Specular reflection from dielectric surfaces (glass) and scattering by particles both impose strong polarization signatures largely invisible to RGB sensors. [HYPOTHESIS] Part of the hard-domain gap may be an information deficit of the sensing modality, not a modeling deficit, which is decidable by comparing modest polarization-equipped models against the best RGB-only models on matched scenes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On matched capture sets, a small model with polarimetric input outperforms the strongest available RGB foundation models on transparent-surface and smoke delineation, and the advantage concentrates exactly on cases RGB models fail bimodally, demonstrating the bottleneck is sensing information, not model capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The polarization-small versus RGB-large comparison will favor polarization on hard cases despite orders-of-magnitude capacity difference; RGB-large dominance falsifies the information-gap claim.
why_important: It would redirect investment from ever-larger RGB models toward sensor-model co-design for this territory, with immediate implications for robotics and fire monitoring hardware.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Polarimetric vision exists as a field; a capacity-controlled information-gap adjudication against foundation models may be new framing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture a co-registered polarimetric and RGB dataset of glass and smoke scenes, train small polarimetric models, evaluate the best RGB models on the RGB channel, and compare on hard-case strata.
main_risk: Polarization cameras are less common; dataset scale will be small, inviting sample-size critiques on the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Scaling RGB models is assumed to eventually solve transparency and haze perception without new sensors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uncontrolled outdoor polarization (sky polarization, mixed illumination) may be too noisy for small models to exploit reliably outside the lab.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Capture a few dozen lab scenes with a polarization camera, train a tiny probe, and compare with one RGB foundation model within a week.

one_line_idea: Modeling the scanner's point-spread function inside the label likelihood may correct a systematic boundary bias that no amount of data can fix.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Medical images are convolutions of anatomy with a device-specific point-spread function, so observed edges are displaced and blurred versions of true tissue interfaces in a signal-dependent way. [HYPOTHESIS] Training on annotations of the blurred image teaches models the blurred boundary, embedding a device-dependent bias that behaves as an offset, not noise, and therefore cannot be averaged away by data volume.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Incorporating a known or estimated PSF into the segmentation likelihood (predicting pre-blur anatomy that, when convolved, explains the image and annotation) removes a boundary offset that standard training provably retains, with the offset magnitude scaling with PSF width, demonstrable on phantoms and transferable across devices.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] On phantom scans with known geometry across PSF widths, standard training will show boundary offsets growing with PSF width while the PSF-aware twin stays near zero; equal offsets falsify the likelihood-level correction claim.
why_important: Device-dependent boundary bias breaks cross-scanner volume comparability, a core requirement of longitudinal oncology; a formulation-level fix would improve every downstream measurement without new data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] PSF modeling is standard in reconstruction and super-resolution; embedding it in the segmentation training objective as a bias-removal mechanism may be underexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate or scan physical phantoms across blur settings, train standard and PSF-aware twins, and compare signed boundary error versus PSF width.
main_risk: PSF estimation error on real devices may reintroduce comparable bias, capping practical benefit.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Scanner blur is treated as augmentation-addressable noise rather than as a structured bias requiring likelihood modeling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotators may already compensate for blur when contouring, partially pre-correcting labels and shrinking the removable bias.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Measure whether one model's boundary placement shifts systematically across synthetic blur levels of the same phantom in a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke, fog, and haze are points in one scattering-parameter space: regressing physical parameters might generalize where classification fundamentally cannot.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Atmospheric scattering media are characterized by continuous physical parameters (extinction coefficient, single-scattering albedo, particle phase function), with smoke, fog, and haze occupying overlapping regions. [HYPOTHESIS] Training classifiers on discretized media categories may force arbitrary boundaries in a continuous space, guaranteeing brittleness at category borders where physics offers no discontinuity to learn.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Networks trained to regress continuous scattering parameters from images generalize across media categories far better than category classifiers trained on the same scenes, and category decisions derived post hoc from regressed parameters match or beat direct classification even in-domain, showing the categorical formulation was the bottleneck.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-media transfer (train mostly on fog-like, test on smoke-like parameters) will strongly favor the regression formulation; equal transfer falsifies the continuous-space account.
why_important: It would replace an endless per-category data collection race with a physically grounded shared representation for all participating media, directly serving fire, weather, and pollution applications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Physics-based dehazing estimates transmission; framing media identity itself as parameter regression with cross-category generalization tests may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render media across a parameter grid, train regression and classification twins, evaluate cross-region generalization and derived-category accuracy.
main_risk: Parameter ground truth exists only synthetically; real-data validation must rely on weak labels (visibility measurements, co-located sensors).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Media types are treated as semantic categories to be classified like object classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Category-correlated context (fog sits in valleys at dawn; smoke has sources) may carry more usable signal than the physics parameters themselves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train both twins on a coarse synthetic parameter grid and compare cross-region error within a few days.

one_line_idea: Smoke casts shadows that encode its optical thickness; models likely ignore this free evidence, and shadow-occlusion counterfactuals can prove it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A smoke plume attenuates sunlight, casting a soft shadow whose darkness maps the plume's column density along light rays. [HYPOTHESIS] This indirect evidence could disambiguate faint plumes from background haze, but current models probably read shadows as unrelated dark regions, discarding a physically informative channel (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Current smoke segmenters derive negligible information from cast shadows: editing shadows out of scenes (or injecting fake plume shadows) leaves plume masks statistically unchanged, whereas an ideal observer analysis on the same scenes shows shadows contain substantial disambiguating information, quantifying an unused evidence channel.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Shadow-editing counterfactuals will produce near-zero mask changes across models while ideal-observer bounds show large shadow information content; strong model sensitivity to shadow edits falsifies the unused-channel claim.
why_important: Faint-plume detection at distance (early wildfire response) is the highest-value smoke problem; an untapped physical evidence channel would offer improvement without new sensors.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Shadow analysis exists for opaque-object detection; treating participating-media shadows as a quantified, unused evidence channel for dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build shadow-edited counterfactual pairs (removal and injection) for plume scenes, measure model mask sensitivity, and compute an information-content estimate for the shadow channel via a trained shadow-only probe.
main_risk: Clean shadow editing on real images is hard; renders may be needed, importing sim-to-real caveats.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Shadows are nuisance illumination variation to be invariant against, not evidence to be exploited.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Shadow evidence may be too entangled with terrain albedo variation for even ideal observers to extract reliably outdoors.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inject synthetic plume shadows into ten clear scenes and check whether any model's smoke output moves at all within a day.

one_line_idea: Structured backgrounds make glass physically easier (refraction reveals it), but models may perform identically on structured and plain backgrounds, proving they skip the physics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Refraction through glass displaces the image of a structured background in a geometrically lawful way, making glass much more physically detectable against texture than against blank walls. [HYPOTHESIS] If models exploited refractive evidence, their performance would be strongly background-dependent in the physically predicted direction; flat dependence would reveal that learned perception ignores available physics entirely.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Model performance on transparent objects is nearly independent of background structure richness, while ideal-observer difficulty varies enormously with it, and this performance-difficulty decoupling is a quantitative signature of physics-blind recognition by contour and context.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The correlation between per-scene background structure and per-scene model performance will be near zero despite large physical detectability variation; strong positive correlation falsifies the physics-blindness claim.
why_important: The decoupling measurement establishes how far learned perception sits from physical optimality per scene type, and predicts which deployment scenes (blank labs versus textured homes) will not behave as benchmarks suggest.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Performance-versus-physical-informativeness decoupling as an audit statistic for learned dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Render or capture matched glass scenes over background-structure sweeps, measure model performance versus a physics-based detectability index, and quantify the coupling.
main_risk: Background structure also affects contour visibility, partially confounding the physics channel with the shortcut channel.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Better models are assumed to gradually pick up all usable cues, including refraction, as data grows.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some coupling may exist through indirect pathways (structured backgrounds sharpen contours), producing correlation without genuine refraction use.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one model on glass against five background types and correlate performance with a crude structure index in a day.

one_line_idea: Smoke is a process, not an object: tiny temporal models may beat huge single-frame foundation models at equal compute because the signal lives in dynamics.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Turbulent plumes have characteristic spatiotemporal statistics (advective coherence, eddy turnover) absent from any single frame. [HYPOTHESIS] The field's investment in single-frame foundation capability may be misallocated for process-like targets: the discriminative information may be overwhelmingly temporal, making frame-based scaling a losing strategy for this class.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched inference compute, small models consuming short temporal windows outperform the largest single-frame models on faint-smoke segmentation by a wide margin, and the advantage grows as opacity decreases, establishing that for participating media the information bottleneck is temporal access, not model capacity.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The compute-matched comparison will show temporal-small dominating frame-large on low-opacity strata; frame-large winning everywhere falsifies the temporal-information claim.
why_important: It would redirect architecture and benchmark design for the entire smoke-fire area toward temporal formulations and reveal a general lesson about process-like versus object-like target classes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Video segmentation exists, but a compute-matched information-location adjudication between temporal access and model scale on process-like classes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix inference compute budgets, train small temporal-window models and evaluate against large frame models on opacity-stratified smoke video benchmarks.
main_risk: Compute matching across fundamentally different architectures is contestable and must be defined transparently (latency, FLOPs, or energy).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Stronger single-frame backbones are assumed the primary path, with temporal modeling as a secondary refinement.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Large frame models may extract subtle static texture (haze microstructure) that equals the temporal channel, especially at higher opacities.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare one small temporal model against one large frame model on a faint-smoke subset without full compute sweeps, as a directional pilot within days.

one_line_idea: Combustion imposes characteristic flicker dynamics on flames; frame-trained models cannot represent them, and the deficit is measurable as a specific hard-negative failure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Buoyant diffusion flames oscillate with characteristic low-frequency flicker governed by combustion physics. [HYPOTHESIS] The hardest fire false positives (sunset reflections, flame-colored fabric, screens showing fire) are static or differently dynamic, so temporal flicker is the discriminating variable that frame-based systems structurally lack; the size of this deficit on hard negatives is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On a hard-negative suite of flame-like static and dynamic confusers, frame-based models exhibit high false-positive rates that temporal models reduce dramatically by exploiting flicker statistics, and the false positives that remain for temporal models are precisely confusers sharing flame-like temporal spectra (true reflections of real fire), confirming the spectral mechanism.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The false-positive reduction from temporal input will concentrate on spectrally non-flame confusers, with reflection-type confusers remaining; uniform reduction across confuser types falsifies the spectral-mechanism claim.
why_important: False alarms dominate the practical cost of fire detection systems; a mechanistic account of which confusers temporal modeling can and cannot reject enables honest deployment specifications.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Flicker-based classical fire detection exists in signal-processing literature; a mechanistic hard-negative decomposition for modern dense predictors may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Curate hard negatives with measured temporal spectra (static flame-alikes, reflections of real flames, screens), evaluate frame and temporal models, and stratify false positives by confuser spectrum.
main_risk: Reflections of real fire genuinely carry flame spectra, so full rejection is physically impossible and the evaluation must define success accordingly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Better appearance features are assumed sufficient for rejecting flame-like confusers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern frame models may exploit subtle static cues (glare geometry, context) achieving low false positives without any temporal channel.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Test one frame model on twenty static flame-like confusers and count false fires in an afternoon to size the problem.

one_line_idea: If smoke-extent ambiguity is structured rather than noisy, temporal averaging of predictions will not shrink it at the rate independent noise predicts; the deviation measures ambiguity structure.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Aggregating predictions across frames is the default remedy for unstable extent estimates, implicitly assuming per-frame errors are independent noise. If the penumbra ambiguity is a stable structural property, aggregation will converge quickly to a biased answer, and the convergence rate itself becomes a diagnostic of ambiguity type (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance of temporally aggregated extent estimates decays much slower than the reciprocal of frame count for smoke (structured ambiguity) but near-nominally for crisp moving objects (independent noise), and the decay-rate deficit quantifies the fraction of extent uncertainty that is structural and cannot be averaged away.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Log-variance versus log-frame-count curves will show slope deficits for smoke well below the independent-noise slope; nominal slopes falsify the structured-ambiguity claim.
why_important: It tells practitioners the hard limit of temporal smoothing for participating media and provides a cheap field diagnostic separating reducible from irreducible extent uncertainty in deployed systems.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Convergence-rate analysis of prediction aggregation as an ambiguity-typing instrument may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On stabilized smoke and control videos, compute extent estimates per frame from fixed models, fit variance-decay slopes across aggregation windows, and compare against the independence benchmark.
main_risk: True scene changes (plume evolution) contaminate the stationarity assumption; the analysis needs quasi-stationary clips or drift correction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] More frames are assumed to steadily improve extent estimates, treating temporal averaging as universally beneficial.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Frame-to-frame model errors are already known to be correlated through shared weights; the field may consider the slower decay unsurprising, reducing novelty to the quantification itself.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute the decay curve for one model on three stabilized smoke clips versus three object clips in a day.

one_line_idea: Optical-flow-based pseudo-labeling breaks on participating media: flow tracks the background through smoke, making motion supervision anti-correlated with the medium.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Optical flow estimates dominant apparent motion, and through semi-transparent media the background's motion often dominates the compositional signal. [HYPOTHESIS] Motion-based self-supervision and pseudo-labeling pipelines, built on the assumption that coherent motion identifies objects, may systematically assign smoke pixels to background motion layers, injecting anti-labels rather than labels for exactly this territory.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In standard motion-segmentation pseudo-labeling pipelines applied to smoke scenes, the medium is assigned to the background layer at a rate far exceeding chance, and models trained on such pseudo-labels perform worse on smoke than models trained with no motion supervision at all, demonstrating actively harmful supervision.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The pseudo-label audit will show systematic background assignment of smoke, and the training comparison will show negative transfer from motion supervision; neutral or positive transfer falsifies the anti-supervision claim.
why_important: Self-supervised video pipelines are being scaled industrially; identifying a class of targets where the core assumption inverts prevents silent contamination of foundation training and explains downstream deficits.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Flow limitations on transparency are known in the flow literature; tracing their consequences through pseudo-labeling into learned segmentation deficits may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a standard motion pseudo-labeling pipeline on smoke-containing videos, audit layer assignments of the medium, then train matched models with and without the motion supervision and compare smoke performance.
main_risk: Multiple pipeline variants exist; critics can claim better flow or layered-motion methods avoid the failure, requiring coverage of representative variants.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Motion cues are considered reliably helpful supervision for video segmentation across classes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Layered flow formulations may partially capture medium motion, making the contamination weaker than hypothesized.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Audit layer assignment of smoke pixels for one pipeline on five clips in a day.

one_line_idea: Predicting spread-rate fields instead of extent masks: the derivative of the process may be more annotator-stable and decision-relevant than its instantaneous state.
