problem: [HYPOTHESIS] For dynamic media, downstream decisions (evacuation, suppression) depend on where the smoke or fire is going, while annotation and evaluation fixate on where it is, which is exactly the ill-posed quantity; whether humans agree more about local spread direction and rate than about instantaneous extent is an open, decision-relevant question.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Inter-annotator agreement on local spread vectors (direction and rate of the advancing front over a short interval) is substantially higher than agreement on instantaneous extent for the same scenes, and models trained on spread targets achieve higher agreement with held-out consensus than extent-trained models retrofitted to spread estimation.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The annotation study will show a large agreement gap favoring spread over extent; equal or reversed agreement falsifies the stability claim and undermines the reformulation.
why_important: If the process derivative is the stable observable, benchmarks and products for fire and smoke should target it directly, resolving the extent-ambiguity problem by changing the question rather than the model.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Front-propagation estimation exists in geoscience contexts; reframing dense prediction targets around annotator-stable process derivatives may be new for this territory.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a two-condition annotation study (extent versus spread vectors on short clips), quantify agreement per condition, then train models on each target and compare consensus agreement.
main_risk: Spread annotation requires new tooling and instructions; poor tooling could depress agreement and bias the comparison against the hypothesis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Extent masks are treated as the canonical target from which any dynamic quantity can be derived by differencing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Differencing ambiguous extents may cancel shared ambiguity, making derived spread as stable as directly annotated spread and the reformulation unnecessary.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pilot both annotation conditions with three annotators on ten clips and compare agreement statistics within days.

one_line_idea: Object-permanence priors in video models may actively harm dissipating-target tracking: memory mechanisms could hold onto smoke that no longer exists.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Video segmentation architectures increasingly use memory and tracking mechanisms embodying object permanence. Smoke and steam violate permanence by dissipating; memory may therefore produce persistent phantom masks after dissipation, a failure mode with direct false-alarm costs that has not been isolated (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Memory-equipped video segmenters exhibit systematic lag in releasing dissipated media (phantom persistence time growing with memory depth), while memoryless per-frame models release immediately, and the persistence artifact transfers across scenes, establishing permanence priors as the cause rather than appearance residue.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Dissipation-sequence evaluations will show phantom persistence proportional to memory capacity across architectures; equal persistence with and without memory falsifies the permanence-prior account.
why_important: Dissipation timing matters (all-clear decisions after incidents); more broadly it exposes a class mismatch between object-centric temporal priors and process-like targets, informing video-foundation design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Memory mechanisms are evaluated on permanence-respecting benchmarks; a dissipation stress test isolating permanence-prior harm may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble or render dissipation sequences with ground-truth end times, evaluate matched memory and memoryless models, and measure mask-release lag versus memory configuration.
main_risk: Faint residual smoke may genuinely persist beyond human annotation, making ground-truth end times contestable without physical measurement.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Temporal memory is assumed to monotonically improve video segmentation robustness.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention-based memories may adapt quickly to disappearance, showing negligible lag and confining the issue to naive persistence heuristics.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one memory-based and one per-frame model on five dissipation clips and compare release timing in a day.

one_line_idea: Event cameras may separate real flames from reflections of flames by capturing combustion microdynamics invisible at standard frame rates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Event sensors report per-pixel brightness changes with sub-millisecond latency, capturing high-frequency dynamics standard cameras integrate away. [HYPOTHESIS] Reflections and screen displays of fire pass through optical and electronic transfer functions that alter high-frequency temporal statistics, so an event-domain signature may distinguish primary combustion from secondary reproductions, the canonical unsolved false-alarm pair.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Event-stream statistics over flame regions occupy a signature regime distinct from reflected or displayed fire in ways learnable by small classifiers with high accuracy, while frame-based inputs at standard rates cannot separate the pair, demonstrating a modality-specific solution to a modality-created problem.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Matched captures of direct flames, reflections, and screen playbacks will be separable in event statistics but not in frame statistics; failure of event-domain separation falsifies the signature claim.
why_important: Reflections and screens are leading false-alarm sources for camera-based fire systems in buildings; a physically grounded discriminator would remove a deployment blocker that appearance modeling cannot address.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Event-based flame detection has appeared in niche engineering contexts (unverified); the specific direct-versus-reproduction separation framing may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capture a controlled rig with co-mounted event and frame cameras viewing direct flames, mirror reflections, and screen playbacks; compare separability under matched classifiers per modality.
main_risk: Screen refresh artifacts trivially separate displays; the mirror-reflection arm is the scientifically decisive and harder comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Reflection false alarms are treated as a context-reasoning problem for smarter appearance models.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Good mirrors may preserve temporal statistics faithfully enough that even event streams cannot separate primary from reflected flames.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One afternoon lab session with a candle, a mirror, and an event camera comparing event-rate spectra of direct versus reflected regions.

one_line_idea: Longitudinal context may collapse margin ambiguity in medical segmentation: growth direction could disambiguate boundaries that single scans cannot.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Margin ambiguity in a single scan may be partially an artifact of missing temporal context: where a lesion is advancing, the ambiguous fringe has a determinate interpretation (active margin) that prior scans reveal. Whether expert disagreement actually shrinks given longitudinal context is measurable and, to my knowledge, unquantified (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Providing raters with registered prior scans reduces inter-rater margin disagreement substantially on infiltrative lesions, and models consuming registered longitudinal pairs reproduce this ambiguity reduction, showing that part of what the field calls aleatoric ambiguity is actually missing-context epistemic uncertainty.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The with-priors annotation condition will show significantly lower rater variance than the single-scan condition on matched cases; no reduction falsifies the missing-context account and confirms the ambiguity as intrinsic.
why_important: Reclassifying part of medical ambiguity from irreducible to context-resolvable changes both clinical annotation protocols and the ceiling estimates used to judge model progress in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Longitudinal segmentation models exist; using longitudinal context as an instrument to decompose ambiguity types in the label distribution may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a within-subjects multi-rater study on infiltrative lesions with and without registered priors, quantify variance reduction, then train matched single-scan and longitudinal models against multi-rater targets.
main_risk: Registration errors between scans introduce their own ambiguity, potentially masking the context benefit.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Rater disagreement on margins is treated as irreducible aleatoric ambiguity setting the performance ceiling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Raters may anchor on priors without genuine information gain, reducing variance spuriously while accuracy against pathology ground truth stays flat.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pilot the two-condition annotation with three raters on fifteen longitudinal cases within a week.

one_line_idea: A fixed two-layer decomposition (medium plus background) may resolve most single-label errors in scenes with participating media, measuring the representational ceiling of flat segmentation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] In scenes with smoke or haze, most pixels simultaneously show the medium and the scene behind it. [HYPOTHESIS] Flat single-label segmentation must pick one, so a large fraction of its measured error in such scenes may be representational, quantifiable by re-scoring under a two-layer output space.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-decoding the same frozen features into a two-layer output (medium opacity layer plus background semantics layer) reclassifies a majority of smoke-scene errors as correct-under-representation, and the residual error better predicts downstream task failure than the original flat error did, establishing the flat label space as the dominant error source in participating-media scenes.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The share of flat-segmentation error resolved by two-layer re-decoding will be large on media scenes and near zero on clear scenes; small resolution shares on media scenes falsify the representational-ceiling claim.
why_important: It quantifies exactly how much of the hard-domain gap can be recovered by task reformulation alone (no new data, no bigger models), a decisive input for research allocation across this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Layered representations exist in matting and dehazing; using them as an error-accounting audit of flat segmentation benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct media-scene evaluations with layered ground truth (renders and composites), decode one frozen backbone under flat and two-layer heads, and partition flat errors by whether the layered head resolves them.
main_risk: Layered ground truth on real (non-composited) scenes is scarce, limiting the real-data arm to weak validation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Segmentation errors in smoky scenes are read as perception failures, and the flat label space is retained unquestioned.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmark conventions (always label the medium when visible) may make flat labels self-consistent enough that little error is genuinely representational.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Manually audit fifty flat-segmentation errors in smoky scenes and count how many are plausible background-layer answers, in one day.

one_line_idea: Boundary ambiguity may be low-dimensional in signed-distance space: rater variation could compress to a few modes, enabling compact ambiguity representations.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-voxel probability maps treat ambiguity as high-dimensional, but if rater contours are smooth deformations of a common shape, ambiguity may live in a low-dimensional subspace of signed-distance perturbations, which would justify far more compact and better-conditioned ambiguity models; the empirical dimensionality is unknown (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Principal-component analysis of rater contour sets in signed-distance representation shows that a handful of modes explains most inter-rater variance for margin-type ambiguity across structures and datasets, and that per-pixel independent uncertainty models waste capacity modeling directions in which no rater variation exists.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The variance-explained curve will be steep (few modes suffice) for margin ambiguity and shallow for topological ambiguity, giving a measurable dimensionality signature; uniformly shallow curves falsify the low-dimensionality claim.
why_important: A validated low-dimensional ambiguity structure would let models output a few shape coefficients with calibrated distributions instead of noisy dense maps, simplifying clinical interfaces and downstream planning integration.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Statistical shape models are classical; using their spectrum as an empirical test of ambiguity dimensionality in modern multi-rater data may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Convert multi-rater contours to signed-distance functions, run PCA per structure class, and report variance-explained spectra stratified by ambiguity type.
main_risk: Signed-distance PCA assumes correspondence and smoothness that fail for topologically variable structures, requiring careful case stratification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Dense per-pixel probabilistic outputs are treated as the natural and necessary representation of segmentation ambiguity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rater variation may include fine-grained idiosyncratic wiggle that PCA in distance space cannot compress, keeping effective dimensionality high.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run the PCA on one multi-rater structure class and inspect the spectrum in a few hours.

one_line_idea: Occupancy and opacity are conflated in smoke labels: annotators answer different questions on different pixels, and decomposing the two could resolve apparent label inconsistency.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] A smoke label can mean smoke is present here (occupancy) or smoke meaningfully obstructs here (opacity); annotators may switch criteria across pixels and images, creating label inconsistency that models cannot fit and evaluations cannot interpret; the conflation has not been isolated as a measurable label defect (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-annotating a smoke subset with separate occupancy and opacity questions reveals that a substantial fraction of apparent inter-annotator disagreement under the standard protocol is criterion disagreement (annotators answering different questions consistently), not perceptual disagreement, and models trained on the decomposed labels show better cross-dataset transfer because the target semantics are finally well-defined.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Disagreement under decomposed annotation will be much lower per question than under standard annotation on matched pixels; equal disagreement falsifies the criterion-conflation account.
why_important: It would identify a fixable protocol defect underlying smoke benchmark noise and provide semantically clean targets that downstream users (visibility estimation, alarm logic) actually need.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Matting separates alpha from segmentation, but diagnosing criterion conflation as a source of measured inter-annotator disagreement in participating-media datasets may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Design a two-question annotation protocol, re-annotate a benchmark subset with multiple raters per question, and decompose standard-protocol disagreement into criterion versus perceptual components.
main_risk: The two questions may be too correlated in practice for annotators to separate, collapsing the decomposition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Smoke label noise is attributed to boundary vagueness, with the question being asked assumed unambiguous.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary vagueness may dominate so strongly that criterion clarity buys little reduction in disagreement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pilot both protocols on ten images with three raters and compare disagreement structures within days.

one_line_idea: Decoder upsampling architecture may impose a high-frequency prior that actively fights soft-boundary targets; frequency-response analysis of decoders could expose it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Common decoder designs (transposed convolutions, pixel shuffle, skip connections from early layers) shape the spatial-frequency content of outputs. [HYPOTHESIS] These designs were tuned for crisp-edge reconstruction and may be structurally biased against the smooth low-frequency transitions that faithful amorphous-boundary prediction requires, a mismatch never characterized as a frequency-domain phenomenon (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Measuring decoder transfer characteristics (output frequency content given controlled feature perturbations) reveals systematic high-frequency amplification, and this amplification quantitatively predicts each architecture's error on soft-boundary targets while being uncorrelated with crisp-target error, isolating a component of hard-domain failure that lives entirely in the decoder design.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Across decoder families, a high-frequency amplification index will correlate strongly with soft-target error and weakly with crisp-target error; absence of the differential correlation falsifies the frequency-mismatch claim.
why_important: It would locate part of the hard-domain gap in a component the field considers task-neutral plumbing, and yield a cheap design rule (frequency-matched decoders) for every soft-boundary application.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Frequency analyses exist for GAN artifacts and implicit representations; a decoder frequency-response audit tied to amorphous segmentation error may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Characterize frequency responses of several standard decoders on fixed backbones, then correlate response indices with soft versus crisp target errors across matched training runs.
main_risk: Nonlinearity makes frequency response input-dependent; the characterization needs careful operating-point definitions to be meaningful.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Decoders are considered interchangeable plumbing, with hard-domain failures attributed to encoders, data, and losses.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training may adapt decoder weights enough to neutralize architectural frequency biases, leaving no measurable link to soft-target error.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare two decoder types trained identically on one soft-target synthetic task and inspect output frequency spectra against ground truth in two days.

one_line_idea: Patch tokenization may quantize extent estimates in patch-size units on low-contrast boundaries, leaving a periodic fingerprint in error histograms.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Vision transformers process images in fixed-size patches. [HYPOTHESIS] Where boundary evidence is weak (faint smoke, subtle lesion margins), the decoder may default to patch-aligned decisions, quantizing predicted extents in patch units, a systematic artifact that would be invisible in aggregate metrics but decisive for fine measurement applications (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Signed boundary-error distributions of transformer-based segmenters on low-contrast boundaries exhibit periodic structure at the patch frequency (and its harmonics), absent in convolutional models and absent on high-contrast boundaries, demonstrating tokenization-induced quantization of dense outputs exactly where evidence is weakest.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Spectral analysis of boundary-error histograms will show significant patch-frequency peaks only for transformer models on weak boundaries; missing peaks falsify the quantization claim.
why_important: Patch-size periodic bias would corrupt volumetric measurements (tumor growth) and extent trends (plume growth) in a correlated way that averaging cannot remove, directly affecting measurement validity in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Tokenization artifacts are studied for reconstruction quality; boundary-error periodicity as an evidence-dependent quantization signature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate matched transformer and convolutional segmenters on stimuli with controlled boundary contrast sweeps, compute signed boundary-error spectra per contrast level, and test for patch-frequency peaks.
main_risk: Positional-embedding interpolation and overlapping patch variants may smear the periodicity, weakening the signature even if quantization occurs.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Modern decoders are assumed to restore full spatial resolution, with tokenization treated as an internal detail without output-space consequences.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Learned upsampling may genuinely interpolate sub-patch boundaries using context, eliminating quantization even on weak evidence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compute boundary-error spectra for one transformer segmenter on a synthetic contrast sweep in a day.

one_line_idea: Partial coverage and uncertainty are confounded in soft masks: a probability of one half can mean half-covered or fully-unknown, and the two need different downstream actions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A soft value in a predicted mask can encode physical partial coverage (thin smoke genuinely at half opacity) or epistemic doubt (unknown whether opaque smoke is present). [HYPOTHESIS] Current soft outputs collapse these into one number, though downstream consumers must act differently on each; whether models internally distinguish the cases, and whether the distinction is recoverable, is unknown (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on standard soft targets internally entangle coverage and uncertainty irrecoverably (no probe can separate constructed half-coverage from ambiguous-full-coverage stimuli), whereas a two-channel formulation (coverage estimate plus confidence) trained on data where the two factors are independently controlled disentangles them and improves downstream decisions that depend on the distinction.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Probes on standard models will fail to separate matched coverage-versus-uncertainty stimulus pairs, while two-channel models separate them; successful probing of standard models falsifies the irrecoverability claim.
why_important: The coverage-uncertainty distinction determines whether to filter (physical) or to escalate for review (epistemic) in every deployment of this territory, from radiology triage to fire response.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] The aleatoric-epistemic literature addresses related structure, but the physical-coverage-versus-doubt confound specific to participating media and matting-style outputs may be unformalized.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct stimulus pairs where coverage and ambiguity are independently controlled (composited opacity versus degraded evidence), train and probe standard and two-channel models, and compare separability and downstream decision utility.
main_risk: Constructing convincing ambiguous-but-fully-covered stimuli without artifacts is delicate and central to the design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] A single soft map is treated as sufficient expressive output for amorphous targets.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The two factors may be statistically separable from context in practice, letting standard models implicitly disentangle them well enough for downstream needs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Build twenty matched stimulus pairs and test one pretrained soft-output model's separability with a linear probe within days.

one_line_idea: Query-based mask decoders presuppose countable instances; on uncountable media they may fragment continua into phantom instances with a measurable signature.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Query-based segmentation architectures allocate a fixed set of object queries, each intended to bind to one instance. [HYPOTHESIS] Participating media have no instances, so query binding may fragment a continuous plume into arbitrary pieces whose boundaries reflect query-competition dynamics rather than scene content, an architecture-induced artifact class not yet characterized (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] On continuous media, query-based decoders produce fragmentation whose piece boundaries are unstable under tiny input perturbations and correlate with query initialization rather than image structure, while dense-decoder baselines show stable continuous masks, identifying instance-prior fragmentation as a distinct, diagnosable failure mode of the query paradigm on this territory.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Perturbation-instability of fragment boundaries will be far higher for query decoders on media than for dense decoders and than for query decoders on true instances; comparable stability falsifies the query-competition account.
why_important: Query architectures are becoming the default; knowing they carry a structural mismatch with uncountable classes informs both architecture choice for this territory and the design of media-compatible query mechanisms.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Query behavior is analyzed for instance tasks; a fragmentation-instability audit on uncountable media may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched query-based and dense decoders on smoke scenes, apply small input perturbations, and quantify fragment-boundary instability and its correlation with query identity across seeds.
main_risk: Semantic-segmentation configurations of query models merge queries per class, potentially hiding the fragmentation the panoptic configuration would show.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Query-based decoders are treated as universally superior successors to dense decoders across all segmentation settings.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Class-level query aggregation may fully absorb the instance prior, making the media pathology unobservable in practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Perturb five smoke images slightly and compare fragment stability of one query-based model against one dense model in a day.

one_line_idea: Predicting the level-set family instead of one mask: supervising all thresholds of a soft target simultaneously may regularize amorphous learning better than any single-threshold label.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Binary supervision throws away the ordering information among pixels (which regions are more smoke-like than others), which for amorphous media is most of the signal; whether ordering-complete supervision (monotone level-set families) changes learning dynamics and generalization on hard domains is untested as a controlled question (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Training with a monotonicity-constrained level-set objective (the model must produce a consistent nested family reproducing soft-target orderings) yields better cross-dataset generalization on amorphous classes than binary or unconstrained soft regression at matched capacity, because the ordering constraint encodes the physically correct structure of the target without committing to any threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-dataset transfer comparisons will favor the level-set-supervised twin on amorphous classes while showing no advantage on crisp classes; uniform results falsify the ordering-structure claim.
why_important: It reframes what supervision should preserve for amorphous targets (order, not threshold) and offers a threshold-free training principle compatible with any downstream operating point.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Ordinal and monotonic constraints exist elsewhere in machine learning; a nested level-set supervision principle for participating-media dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement the three supervision variants on one backbone with matched budgets, train on one smoke dataset with soft targets, and evaluate transfer to a second dataset and to synthetic renders with known density.
main_risk: Enforcing nestedness architecturally may constrain capacity in ways that confound the comparison.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Soft regression already captures whatever binary labels miss; additional ordering structure is assumed redundant.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Plain soft regression may implicitly preserve ordering well enough that the explicit constraint adds nothing measurable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train small twins under two of the variants on synthetic data and compare density-ordering fidelity within two days.

one_line_idea: The annotation tool is a hidden co-author of smoke datasets: brush versus polygon tooling may leave decodable signatures that models then learn as target structure.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Annotation interfaces differ (polygon clicking, brush painting, smart-select tools), and their affordances shape mask geometry. [HYPOTHESIS] For amorphous targets where the image underdetermines the boundary, tool affordances may dominate the label geometry, meaning datasets teach tool behavior rather than smoke perception; the effect size is unmeasured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The annotation tool used is decodable from mask geometry at high accuracy on amorphous classes (but only weakly on crisp classes), and models trained on single-tool datasets reproduce tool-specific geometry on new images, demonstrating measurable tool-bias inheritance concentrated exactly where image evidence is weakest.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Tool classification from amorphous-class masks will be far above chance and predictions of single-tool-trained models will cluster by training tool; chance-level decodability falsifies the tool-bias claim.
why_important: Tool bias is a controllable dataset-construction variable; quantifying it would justify tool standardization or tool-diverse annotation as cheap interventions to improve every benchmark in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Annotator bias is studied at the human level; the interface as a distinct causal factor with inheritance measurement may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Re-annotate one image set under controlled tool conditions with rater crossover, train tool classifiers on masks, then train models per tool condition and compare their output geometries.
main_risk: Tool and annotator effects are entangled unless the crossover design is strictly enforced, which increases study cost.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Annotation quality is discussed in terms of annotator skill and guidelines; the interface is treated as neutral.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Guideline and skill variance may dwarf tool effects, leaving tool signatures too weak to matter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Have two raters each label ten smoke images with two tools and test same-day whether a simple classifier separates the tools from geometry.

one_line_idea: The sim-to-real gap for smoke may concentrate in the thin-smoke regime where renderers approximate scattering most aggressively, making synthetic data mis-teach exactly the hard cases.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Real-time and even offline renderers approximate multiple scattering and fine plume microstructure for efficiency. [HYPOTHESIS] These approximations may be most consequential visually in the thin, wispy regime that is also the operationally critical regime (early detection), so synthetic training data could be systematically least faithful precisely where models most need it; the regime structure of the sim-to-real gap is unmeasured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained on synthetic smoke show a sim-to-real transfer gap that is strongly opacity-dependent, largest at low opacity, and traceable to identifiable renderer approximations (scattering order, noise spectra), so improving renderer fidelity only in the thin regime recovers most of the transfer loss at a fraction of the rendering cost.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Opacity-stratified transfer evaluation will show the gap concentrating at low opacity, and targeted fidelity improvements will close it disproportionately; a flat gap across opacity falsifies the regime-concentration claim.
why_important: Synthetic data is the main scaling path for smoke perception; knowing where the gap lives converts blind data scaling into targeted fidelity engineering with direct early-detection payoff.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Sim-to-real analyses usually report aggregate gaps; a physically stratified gap decomposition with targeted-fidelity intervention may be new for participating media.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train on synthetic smoke from renderers at several fidelity settings, evaluate on real footage stratified by estimated opacity, and map the gap against regime and renderer configuration.
main_risk: Estimating opacity strata on real footage requires a proxy whose errors could blur the stratification.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] The sim-to-real gap is treated as a uniform domain shift addressed by domain randomization and adaptation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The dominant gap may be background and lighting realism rather than medium rendering, making opacity stratification irrelevant.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Evaluate one synthetic-trained model on real clips binned by rough visibility of background through smoke and inspect the gap profile within days.

one_line_idea: Sparse physical sensor labels (particulate, thermal) may beat dense human labels per unit cost for training calibrated smoke extent models.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Human annotation of smoke is expensive, threshold-ambiguous, and dense; co-located physical sensors (particulate counters, thermal cameras, lidar) provide sparse but objective point measurements. The label-efficiency and calibration trade-off between subjective-dense and objective-sparse supervision has not been mapped for this territory (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For calibrated extent and density estimation (as opposed to benchmark IoU against human masks), models trained on sparse physical labels plus unlabeled images dominate models trained on equal-cost dense human annotation, because objective point supervision anchors the physical scale that human thresholds cannot provide.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Cost-matched training comparisons evaluated against held-out physical measurements will favor sensor-supervised models on calibration metrics; human-label dominance on those metrics falsifies the claim.
why_important: It would redefine data collection strategy for smoke perception around instrumented capture campaigns rather than annotation farms, with calibration benefits no human labels can deliver.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Weak supervision from sensors exists in other domains; a rigorous cost-matched comparison against human annotation for participating-media dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument controlled smoke releases with co-located sensors and cameras, create cost-matched supervision sets (sensor-sparse versus human-dense), train matched models, and evaluate against independent physical measurements.
main_risk: Sensor-to-pixel correspondence (projecting point measurements into image space) introduces geometric and temporal alignment errors that could sink the sparse arm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Dense human masks are treated as the gold standard supervision, with sensors relegated to evaluation roles at best.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense spatial coverage may matter more than objective scale for learnability, letting human labels win despite their threshold subjectivity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Use existing thermal-visible paired footage to train a small model on thermal-derived sparse labels and compare against a human-label twin on physical plausibility checks within a week.

one_line_idea: Asking annotators for explicit dont-know bands may buy more calibration per annotation dollar than collecting more raters.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] The standard route to ambiguity-aware labels is aggregating many raters, which is expensive and conflates criterion differences with perception. Directly eliciting each rater's uncertain band (tri-map style: definitely-in, definitely-out, unsure) might capture the ambiguity structure with one rater; the budget-matched comparison between the two elicitation strategies is missing (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At matched annotation budget, single-rater tri-map elicitation produces training targets that yield better-calibrated models on ambiguous boundaries than multi-rater binary aggregation, because the unsure band directly encodes the quantity that multi-rater variance only estimates noisily through few samples.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Budget-matched training comparisons will show superior boundary calibration for tri-map-trained models against held-out many-rater consensus distributions; multi-rater superiority falsifies the direct-elicitation claim.
why_important: Annotation budget allocation is a first-order practical decision for every hard-domain dataset builder; a validated cheaper route to calibrated ambiguity would change dataset construction across medical and safety domains.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Tri-maps exist in matting and uncertain-region labels appear occasionally; a controlled budget-matched elicitation-strategy comparison for calibration outcomes may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect both label types on the same images at matched cost plus a large-rater-count reference set, train matched models on each, and compare calibration against the reference ambiguity distribution.
main_risk: Rater unsure bands may reflect personality (confidence styles) more than stimulus ambiguity, adding a new bias axis.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] More raters is treated as the canonical path to ambiguity ground truth.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Self-reported uncertainty is known in psychology to be poorly calibrated (KNOWN FACT at the general level), which may transfer to spatial bands and ruin the direct elicitation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Pilot both strategies on twenty images and compare the unsure bands against a five-rater disagreement map within a week.

one_line_idea: A measurable share of cross-site medical performance drop may be label-convention shift, isolable by re-contouring a subset under a unified protocol.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Models degrade when evaluated on data from new institutions, conventionally attributed to image distribution shift. [HYPOTHESIS] Part of this drop may be the evaluation labels changing convention (different contouring habits), not the model getting worse at anatomy; the decomposition of cross-site drop into image-shift and label-shift components is rarely if ever measured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-contouring a target-site evaluation subset by source-site-convention annotators recovers a substantial fraction of the measured cross-site performance drop, proving that current transfer numbers conflate model degradation with ground-truth redefinition and overstate the image-shift problem.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Performance against convention-matched re-contours will sit measurably above performance against native target-site labels; no recovery falsifies the label-shift component for that pairing.
why_important: Domain adaptation research allocates effort based on cross-site drop magnitudes; if a chunk is label artifact, harmonizing protocols is cheaper than adapting models, and reported generalization failures need reinterpretation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Site harmonization is discussed for images; a controlled label-side decomposition of transfer drops via convention-matched re-annotation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select two sites with a known performance drop, commission re-contouring of a target-site subset by source-convention experts, and re-evaluate to decompose the drop.
main_risk: Recruiting annotators who authentically embody a site's convention, rather than their own style, may be infeasible.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Cross-site drops are read entirely as model brittleness under image distribution shift.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For structures with tight contouring guidelines, conventions may be effectively identical across sites, leaving nothing to recover.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Have one source-site expert re-contour twenty target-site cases and measure the evaluation delta within a week.

one_line_idea: Active learning in ambiguous domains may spend its budget on irreducibly ambiguous pixels; separating ambiguity from epistemic uncertainty could double acquisition efficiency.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Standard acquisition functions select high-uncertainty samples. [HYPOTHESIS] In domains where much uncertainty is irreducible ambiguity (soft boundaries, rater disagreement), these functions may systematically select pixels whose labels are noise, wasting budget and possibly harming the model; the size of this misallocation in hard domains is unmeasured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In smoke and medical segmentation, a large fraction of pixels selected by standard uncertainty acquisition falls in high-rater-disagreement regions where additional labels add noise rather than signal, and an acquisition function that discounts estimated ambiguity achieves equivalent performance with substantially less annotation, quantifying the ambiguity tax on active learning.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Budget-matched active learning comparisons will show the ambiguity-discounting policy dominating standard acquisition on hard domains while matching it on crisp domains; no efficiency gain falsifies the misallocation claim.
why_important: Active learning is the assumed remedy for expensive medical annotation; if it is structurally wasteful exactly in hard domains, correcting the acquisition principle has direct cost consequences for dataset builders.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Noise-aware active learning exists in classification; measuring the ambiguity tax and validating disambiguated acquisition for hard-domain dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate active learning on multi-rater datasets (rater pool as label oracle), compare standard versus ambiguity-discounting acquisition under matched budgets across hard and crisp domains.
main_risk: Estimating ambiguity before labels exist is the crux; a weak ambiguity estimator collapses the proposed policy into the standard one.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] High-uncertainty samples are treated as the most informative by definition.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Labels in ambiguous regions may still constrain the decision boundary usefully, making the ambiguity tax smaller than feared.
fastest_falsification_experiment: On one multi-rater dataset, measure what fraction of top-uncertainty pixels lie in top-disagreement regions in a few hours.

one_line_idea: Copy-paste augmentation is physically invalid for participating media: pasted smoke without recomputed attenuation may teach models compositing artifacts as the cue.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Copy-paste augmentation composites source regions onto new backgrounds without modeling light transport; for opaque objects this is roughly valid, but pasted smoke should attenuate and scatter light from its new background and does not. [HYPOTHESIS] Models trained with such augmentation may learn compositing signatures (boundary statistics, illumination inconsistency) as smoke evidence, degrading real-world performance while inflating validation scores on similarly composited data.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Smoke models trained with naive copy-paste augmentation respond more strongly to compositing artifacts than to physical smoke cues (verified by artifact-only probes), and physically corrected compositing (attenuation-aware blending) removes this artifact reliance while preserving augmentation benefits, isolating a data-pipeline cause of real-world brittleness.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Artifact-only probe images (compositing signature without smoke appearance) will trigger naive-augmented models but not physically-augmented ones; equal responses falsify the artifact-learning claim.
why_important: Copy-paste is a default augmentation across dense prediction; establishing physical validity conditions for participating media would correct a silent contamination in the training pipelines of this whole territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Copy-paste artifacts are discussed for instance segmentation; a physical-validity analysis specific to translucent media with artifact-probe methodology may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train twins with naive versus attenuation-aware compositing augmentation, construct artifact-only and smoke-only probe sets, and compare cue reliance and real-footage transfer.
main_risk: Attenuation-aware compositing requires estimating background depth and lighting, and errors there may introduce different artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Copy-paste is treated as a harmless, broadly beneficial augmentation for any class.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may generalize past compositing artifacts given enough real data, making the contamination negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Probe one existing composite-augmented model with boundary-artifact-only stimuli and check for false activations within a day.

one_line_idea: Near-duplicate video frames may contaminate smoke and fire benchmark splits, inflating reported performance; temporal-split audits could measure the inflation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Many smoke and fire datasets are built by sampling frames from a limited set of source videos. [HYPOTHESIS] Random train-test splitting over frames then places near-duplicates across the split boundary, letting models memorize scenes rather than generalize; the magnitude of this inflation for this territory's benchmarks is unmeasured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-evaluating published-style models under strict source-video-disjoint splits reduces measured performance substantially relative to frame-random splits on the same data, and the reduction correlates with per-dataset duplication statistics, quantifying how much of reported smoke-fire progress is split leakage.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The video-disjoint re-evaluation will show large performance reductions on datasets with high near-duplicate rates and small reductions on genuinely diverse datasets; uniform small reductions falsify the leakage-inflation claim.
why_important: If headline numbers in this safety-relevant area are leakage-inflated, deployment decisions are being made on optimistic evidence; the audit also yields a concrete split protocol for future benchmarks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Duplicate-leakage audits exist for classification datasets; a systematic split-protocol audit for smoke-fire dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute near-duplicate statistics for public smoke-fire datasets, retrain matched models under frame-random and video-disjoint splits, and report the performance delta per dataset.
main_risk: Source-video metadata may be missing, requiring duplicate detection heuristics whose errors affect the split construction.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Published benchmark numbers are taken at face value as generalization measurements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Some benchmarks may already enforce video-level splits, making the audit confirmatory rather than corrective for those cases.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run perceptual-hash duplicate detection across train-test boundaries of two public datasets in a day to size the contamination before any retraining.

one_line_idea: A boundary-evidence spectrum may organize all hard domains: failure modes may cluster by evidence type (photometric, geometric, semantic) rather than by application domain.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Medical, smoke, and transparency communities work in isolation, each treating its failures as domain-specific. If failure modes are actually organized by the type of boundary evidence available (crisp photometric edge, geometric-only boundary as in glass, semantic-only boundary as in infiltrative tumor, no boundary as in smoke), the territory has a shared structure that would let remedies transfer; this organizing claim is untested (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Error-map statistics (spatial error decompositions, failure signatures) from models across the three domains cluster by boundary-evidence type rather than by domain when analyzed blind, establishing evidence type as the true taxonomy of hard dense prediction and domain identity as a superficial variable.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Unsupervised clustering of failure signatures will recover evidence-type groups crossing domain boundaries; clustering by domain instead falsifies the unifying-spectrum claim.
why_important: A validated cross-domain taxonomy would let three research communities pool methods and data by failure type, multiplying effective research effort on this territory's shared core problem.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Cross-domain failure taxonomies for dense prediction, validated by blind clustering rather than argued conceptually, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Standardize error-signature extraction across representative datasets of each domain, annotate cases by evidence type, run blind clustering, and compare cluster-evidence and cluster-domain alignment.
main_risk: Dataset-specific nuisances (resolution, annotation style) may dominate signatures, requiring aggressive normalization that critics can dispute.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Each hard domain is treated as requiring domain-specific expertise and methods, with cross-domain structure assumed limited.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary-evidence type may be only one of several interacting factors (scale, class frequency, modality), too weak alone to dominate clustering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Extract failure signatures for one model per domain on a handful of cases each and inspect a low-dimensional embedding for evidence-type grouping within days.

one_line_idea: Ambiguity-type transfer may beat domain-appearance transfer: training on smoke might help infiltrative tumor margins more than training on crisp tumors does.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Transfer learning is organized by domain similarity (medical to medical), but if the binding constraint on hard classes is handling a given ambiguity type, then cross-domain transfer within an ambiguity type could exceed within-domain transfer across ambiguity types; this reversal has never been tested as a hypothesis about the structure of transfer (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In a transfer matrix spanning domains (medical, smoke, transparency) and ambiguity types (soft boundary, geometric-only, structural multimodality), source tasks sharing the target's ambiguity type yield better fine-tuned performance on the target's ambiguous regions than same-domain sources of different ambiguity type, showing that what transfers is ambiguity-handling competence, not domain appearance.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The transfer matrix will show ambiguity-type block structure stronger than domain block structure on ambiguous-region metrics; domain-dominant structure falsifies the claim.
why_important: It would rewrite pretraining strategy for this territory: hard-domain practitioners should seek ambiguity-matched sources anywhere rather than domain-matched sources, unlocking abundant non-medical data for medical ambiguity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Transfer studies measure domain and task similarity; ambiguity type as the organizing transfer variable may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a source-target grid over the two factors with matched data sizes, fine-tune consistently, and evaluate ambiguous-region performance to fill the transfer matrix.
main_risk: Confounding between ambiguity type and low-level statistics (soft boundaries correlate with certain textures) may mimic ambiguity-type transfer.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Domain proximity is treated as the primary predictor of transfer success.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Low-level appearance transfer may dominate so strongly that ambiguity competence is a second-order effect invisible in the matrix.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Run one cell comparison (smoke-source versus crisp-medical-source onto infiltrative-margin target) with small models within a week.

one_line_idea: Hard-domain benchmarks may be approaching label-entropy floors: an estimable irreducibility bound could separate real headroom from noise-chasing.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Every benchmark whose labels contain ambiguity has an error floor below which improvement means fitting annotation idiosyncrasy. The field lacks a standard method to estimate this floor for dense prediction, so it cannot say which hard-domain benchmarks have genuine headroom; constructing and validating such an estimator is an open problem (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A label-entropy floor estimated from limited multi-rater subsamples (via disagreement extrapolation models) accurately predicts the plateau level that model performance approaches as capacity and data scale, validated on benchmarks where large rater pools exist, making remaining headroom a measurable quantity rather than a matter of faith.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Scaling-curve plateaus of strong models will match independently estimated entropy floors within tight tolerance across several benchmarks; systematic plateau-floor mismatches falsify the estimator or the floor concept.
why_important: A validated headroom meter would redirect effort away from exhausted benchmarks, justify new data collection where floors are high, and give reviewers an objective tool for judging claimed improvements in this territory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Bayes-error estimation exists for classification; a practical, validated floor estimator for ambiguous dense prediction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On benchmarks with many raters available for a subset, fit disagreement-based floor estimates from few raters, then compare against both held-out full-rater-pool disagreement and observed model plateau levels.
main_risk: Extrapolating rater disagreement from few raters requires assumptions about the rater population that may not hold across institutions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Benchmark improvements are assumed meaningful at any performance level; headroom is not routinely questioned quantitatively.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model errors and rater disagreement may be structurally different, letting models pass through the apparent floor by agreeing with consensus better than raters do individually.
fastest_falsification_experiment: For one multi-rater dataset, compare a two-rater-based floor estimate against the full rater pool's disagreement in a day of analysis.

one_line_idea: A shared learned contrast operator may underlie failures across glass, smoke, and lesions: adversarial contrast perturbations might transfer across all three domains.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] If models across domains rely on a similar internal contrast computation as their primary boundary evidence, then the hard domains fail for one shared mechanistic reason, and perturbations crafted to break contrast processing in one domain should transfer to the others; cross-domain adversarial transfer as a mechanism probe is untested for this territory (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Adversarial perturbations optimized to degrade boundary detection on one hard domain transfer to the other two at rates far exceeding cross-domain transfer measured on crisp-object controls, indicating a shared contrast-processing bottleneck as the common cause of hard-domain failure.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The cross-domain transfer matrix of boundary-targeted perturbations will show elevated transfer among the three hard domains relative to controls; control-level transfer falsifies the shared-mechanism claim.
why_important: Mechanistic unification would mean a single representational fix (contrast-robust boundary computation) could lift all three application areas simultaneously, a rare convergence opportunity.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Adversarial transferability is studied across models and datasets; using it as a probe for shared failure mechanisms across application domains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Craft boundary-targeted perturbations per domain on standard models, measure the full cross-domain transfer matrix including crisp controls, and test for hard-domain block elevation.
main_risk: Adversarial transfer is influenced by architecture similarity; the study must vary architectures to separate mechanism sharing from weight-space artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Failures in different domains are assumed to have different causes requiring different fixes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transfer could reflect generic low-level vulnerability of all dense predictors rather than a specific shared contrast mechanism, demanding careful controls.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Craft perturbations on one glass model and test them on one smoke model against a crisp-control baseline within days.

one_line_idea: Models may fail differently from humans on hard domains in a complementary way, implying human-model teams have more headroom here than anywhere else.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Human contrast sensitivity has a characteristic dependence on spatial frequency, and human perception uses gestalt and knowledge-driven completion. [HYPOTHESIS] If model failure maps on hard domains diverge strongly from psychophysically predicted human failure maps, the two systems fail on complementary cases, which would make hard domains the highest-value setting for human-AI teaming; the complementarity structure is unmeasured (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-case and per-region failure correlations between humans and models are substantially lower on smoke, transparency, and infiltrative-margin tasks than on crisp segmentation tasks, and a simple arbitration rule exploiting the measured complementarity outperforms both alone by a margin unattainable on crisp tasks.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Human-model failure correlation will be markedly lower on hard domains, and team performance gains will track the measured decorrelation; high correlation or absent team gains falsify the complementarity claim.
why_important: It would give a principled, measurable basis for deploying human-in-the-loop systems precisely in this territory, and identify which cases to route to whom.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Human-AI complementarity is studied for classification decisions; failure-map-level complementarity analysis for dense prediction in hard domains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect human segmentations under controlled conditions on hard and crisp task samples, compute failure-map correlations with models, and evaluate simple routing rules built on the measured structure.
main_risk: Human dense annotation under controlled psychophysical conditions is slow, limiting sample sizes for the correlation estimates.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Hard cases are assumed hard for humans and models alike, making teaming gains marginal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both humans and models may fail on the same information-starved cases (the stimulus is the bottleneck), yielding high correlation and no teaming headroom.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Compare human and model failures on thirty hard-domain cases in a pilot to estimate the correlation before scaling the study.

one_line_idea: Partitioning benchmark error into information-absent, information-unused, and definition-absent components: a measurement protocol for what kind of hard each hard case is.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] A hard case can be hard because the image lacks the information (information-absent), because models fail to use available information (information-unused), or because the question has no defined answer (definition-absent). Current benchmarks aggregate all three into one error number, so the field cannot tell which problem it is working on; no measurement protocol exists to partition error this way (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The three components are separately measurable (ideal-observer analyses and sensor upgrades bound information absence; human-with-tools performance bounds usable information; instruction-manipulation and rater studies bound definitional ambiguity), and applying the protocol to this territory's benchmarks will show the components have very different proportions across medical, smoke, and transparency, explaining why remedies transfer poorly.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] The partition protocol applied to several benchmarks will yield stable, reproducible component proportions that differ across domains and predict which intervention type (sensor, model, protocol) helps each benchmark; unstable or non-predictive partitions falsify the protocol's validity.
why_important: It converts hardness from a vague aggregate into an actionable diagnosis, telling each subfield whether to buy sensors, build models, or rewrite annotation protocols, arguably the most decision-relevant measurement this territory lacks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] The three-way conceptual distinction appears scattered across literatures; an operationalized, validated partition protocol for dense prediction benchmarks may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Operationalize each bound on one benchmark per domain (synthetic ideal-observer arm, expert-with-tools arm, instruction-manipulation arm), compute partitions, and test their predictive power for intervention outcomes on held-out method comparisons.
main_risk: Each bound is itself an estimate with assumptions; stacking three imperfect bounds may yield partitions too uncertain to act on.

one_line_idea: Distribution-matching evaluation: a large share of persistent hard-domain errors might be re-scored as acceptable answers under the rater distribution, changing what counts as progress.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Evaluation against a single reference mask scores any deviation as error, even when the prediction matches some plausible expert opinion. The fraction of current model error that lies within the plausible-rater set on hard domains has not been measured, yet it determines how much of the reported gap is real (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Under distribution-matching evaluation (a prediction is correct where it falls within the empirical rater distribution), a substantial fraction of state-of-the-art model error on ambiguous structures disappears, and model rankings change, revealing that current one-mask evaluation systematically misrepresents both absolute and relative performance in this territory.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] Re-scoring several models on multi-rater data will reclassify a large share of ambiguous-region errors as within-distribution and produce ranking shifts; negligible reclassification falsifies the misrepresentation claim.
why_important: If a big share of measured error is disagreement with one arbitrary rater rather than mistake, the field's progress narrative and its method rankings on hard domains both need revision, and evaluation infrastructure should move to distribution-based scoring.

one_line_idea: Directional error asymmetry (under- versus over-segmentation) on ambiguous classes may be loss-induced rather than data-induced, testable by loss-swap experiments across domains.
problem: [HYPOTHESIS] Practitioners report domain-specific directional tendencies (models undershoot wispy smoke; conservative over-contouring in some medical settings), usually attributed to data characteristics. Whether the direction of asymmetry is actually set by the training objective, and thus portable across domains, is a separable causal question that has not been isolated (unverified).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The sign and magnitude of extent-error asymmetry on ambiguous regions follows the loss function across domains: swapping losses between a smoke pipeline and a medical pipeline swaps their characteristic asymmetries, while swapping datasets under a fixed loss preserves them, establishing the objective as the causal source of directional bias in this territory.
falsifiable_prediction: [HYPOTHESIS] In a two-by-two loss-by-domain factorial experiment, asymmetry direction will track loss and not domain; domain-tracking asymmetry falsifies the loss-causation claim.
why_important: Directional bias has asymmetric real-world costs (missed smoke versus false alarm, missed tumor versus overtreatment); locating its cause in the loss makes it directly steerable, giving practitioners a control knob instead of a mystery.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION - novelty unverified] Loss-bias analyses exist per task; a cross-domain factorial causal isolation of asymmetry direction may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the factorial design (two domains, two-plus losses, multiple seeds), measure signed extent errors restricted to ambiguous regions, and attribute asymmetry variance to factors.
main_risk: Interactions between loss and class imbalance across domains may prevent clean factorial attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION about consensus] Directional tendencies are treated as domain folklore (smoke is like this, tumors are like that) rather than as controllable consequences of objectives.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Annotation conventions may impose directional bias upstream of any loss effect, dominating the factorial outcome.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Train small models with two losses on one smoke dataset and check whether asymmetry sign flips with the loss within two days.
